items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comAn outstanding album. The Chilean ensemble Asceta has established itself as one of those collectives you simply have to know if you are a fan of music made with extraordinary care and musicianship. Guided by the creative spirit of Rodrigo Maccioni, the band delivers an album in 2026 that, although there are still several months left in the year, could very well be considered the best Rock in Opposition and avant-prog release of the year. "The Fool Leading The Blind" is the title of the Chileans' third full-length release, an ambitious album that, across fifty three minutes, offers five compositions in which magic, social criticism, and music of the highest caliber take center stage. Everything begins with the album's title track, a twenty one minute suite that can be ominous at times, frenetic at others, and remarkably calm in between. The first three minutes are somewhat contemplative, as something gradually begins to take shape. Strings and drums establish a semi-slow rhythm that slowly builds until, around the four minute mark, the first explosion of rock arrives. Rock in Opposition, indeed, because the criticism directed toward our world and our politics is implicit throughout the piece, and the musicians express it through their constantly shifting yet remarkably intelligent way of communicating. I love the unexpected rhythmic changes, the moments when the energy and pulse suddenly rise, and the way every instrument introduces its own notes and ideas before converging into an incredibly solid composition that eventually leads us toward ecstasy. There is something beautiful about the way these musicians organize themselves to construct their music. I only wish that, as a society, we could demonstrate this same kind of organization when it comes to confronting bad governments and defending our land. After this emotional roller coaster, Asceta offers us the somber "Temple of Mirrors". Its opening minute is somewhat dissonant, with scattered sounds appearing here and there without any clearly defined form. Then, little by little, a structure begins to emerge, bringing clearer sounds and direction. Progressive music, naturally, but also classical music, an endless palette of colors and textures, and a remarkable convergence between acoustic and electric elements, as beautifully demonstrated by the guitar. Strings introduce the creepy and ominous atmosphere of "When They Arrive". Gradually, instruments such as bassoon, drums, and clarinet join the landscape, creating a dark environment in which a sense of unease comes naturally. There are brief bursts of intensity that could easily startle an unsuspecting listener, but there are also moments of harmony in which we can look around and decide which path to take. This is highly visual music, and every listen can inspire completely different stories in the listener's mind. There are passages that evoke After Crying or Art Zoyd. Wonderful. With "Everything Stopped", a frenetic and semi-chaotic rhythm takes over, constantly contrasted by pauses filled with cadence but also nervous energy. The ensemble creates fascinating musical connections. At times the strings take the spotlight, at others the winds or the drums, yet there is always a beautiful cohesion that serves as the thread connecting their performances. The music here is never linear, and that may initially turn away listeners who are not comfortable with such an approach. But once you connect with it, a genuine synergy develops, and it remains intact until the very end of the album. Speaking of endings, this magnificent record concludes with "Memento Mori", a ten minute composition that is colorful and multifaceted, filled with playful changes that bring brightness while contrasting beautifully with darker passages. The bass establishes an ongoing conversation with the clarinet and oboe, and as usual, the Chileans deliver a dose of avant-garde music of the highest caliber, something no fan of this particular musical territory should overlook. A well deserved round of applause for Asceta, lovers of art and natural opposers by conviction. May their talent and passion continue to drive them toward creating music as rewarding as this.
items._genre: avant-prog / Rock in Opposition / chamber music / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 智利乐团Asceta的第三张全长专辑，五首作品跨越五十三分钟，以卓越的器乐编排与高度精密的合奏构筑了一张野心勃勃的前卫摇滚专辑。开篇同名二十一分钟组曲在阴郁、狂暴与宁静之间不断切换，弦乐与鼓点交织出渐进式的张力结构，节奏变化出人意料却始终保持内在逻辑。后半部分曲目引入巴松管、单簧管等古典乐器，音画感极强，黑暗不安的氛围与突发的强度爆发交替出现。乐评指出作品融合了进步摇滚与古典音乐的双重语汇，在原声与电声之间取得了出色平衡，并类比匈牙利乐队After Crying的复杂织体。整体制作展示了极高的音乐家素养，每件乐器都贡献独立的声部线条，最终汇合成统一的整体。

items.body: Pendulum is a singular piano trio featuring French pianist Benoît Delbecq with Danish double bass player Jonas Westergaard and drummer Peter Bruun (both Westergaard and Bruun have collaborated before with fellow Danish pianist Søren Kjærgaard). Bruun initiated this trio in 2024 as part of his ambitious research project exploring new approaches to musical time (Multitemporal movement and embodiment through Rhythmic Design at The Danish National Academy of Music). The Pendulum trio investigates all aspects of this classic format, including the most basic sensibilities of space and time, avoiding rigid structures, allowing instead for balance, elegance and fluidity. It challenges us to listen to its music as resonant arcs or shared fields of presence rather than defined by linear time, and explores new ways to transform free improvisation gravity into groove. Delbeq suggested that the trio will play with the presence of physical pendulums on stage, symbolizing the elasticity of time and giving a sense of pulse. These oscillating bodies guide the subtle, cyclical shifts in the music, which, paradoxically, feels familiar: music that sways and breathes, while finding rhythm in the inevitability of motion. The trio releases its eight-volume EP series, Arcs , nearly three hours of music, in a monthly release cycle that began in May and will conclude in December 2026. These Arcs offer Pendulum’s idiosyncratic, enigmatic, lyrical universe, in which metric relations, shifting balances, and elastic phrasing are woven together in a kaleidoscopic manner. Each volume swings on its own terms, with no intention to offer a linear narrative, and uses distinct compositional fragments, notated and graphic scores. But the whole project accumulates into an open body of work that allows us to feel how time bends, breathes, and searches for an elusive balance. The Pendulum trio invites listeners to form their own path through the eight volumes and discover different insights and relations in their own time. Arc No. 1 Pendulum describes this volume: “Time leans before it moves. Motion unfolds patiently, stretching and rebounding with quiet elasticity. What propels the arc is not force but attentiveness, which allows duration to bend and return without breaking. Each swing carries clarity and restraint, revealing time as something more shaped than measured”. The trio suggests sparse, deep listening, labyrinthine architectures with patient and subtle, cyclical-rhythmic shifts, best captured in the aptly titled, 17-minute minimalist “Exercice Elastique”, that patiently gravitates into a most delicate, vulnerable, quite irreverent groove. Arc No. 2 “Afterwards appears before it is recognized. Movement writes itself into space, leaving subtle traces that guide listening rather than direction. Rhythms form paths, both adaptable and responsive, where perception stretches between memory and anticipation. The arc remains fluid, shaped by change rather than arrival”. Pendulum sketches an almost abstract, empty map, from which it begins to imagine possible contours and paths, and how to find its inner, spatial logic, and its subtle rhythmic shifts, finally realized on “Plasticity”. Arc No. 3 “Movement turns inward. Each gesture is weighted, deliberate, and reduced to necessity. Time thickens as motion slows, inviting attention to settle inside the smallest shifts. The arc transforms discreetly, as intensity is held beneath restraint. Balance is discovered through presence, not display”. The 31-minute “Buto” corresponds with the hyper-slow and hyper-controlled motion of the Japanese avant-dance theatre, Butō (舞踏), that resists and fixated conception of time. Pendulum’s fragile balance was realized through an austere, cryptic, and often almost silent presence that keeps triggering our imagination, and not by technical display or mastery. Arc No. 4 “Wooden time moves with grain and resistance. Motion creaks, sways, and negotiates its own structure. Oscillation becomes tactile, shaped by friction and patience. The arc holds multiple possibilities at once, allowing form and freedom to coexist without resolution. The rings of time are both counted and counting”. The trio focuses on its essence, the ever-negotiated arcs that blur the distinction between form and freedom, and question our conception of linear time, turning it into a spiritual riddle, a kōan. Arc No. 5 “A phase shifts nearly unnoticed. Motion lightens, stepping carefully through softened contours. Layers thin and overlap, revealing phrasing where gestures begin and fade. The arc listens closely to its own balance, finding meaning in nuance rather than emphasis. The push and pull are their own reason for being”. Pendulum refines its fragile, nuanced equilibrium with melodic threads that patiently, hesitantly flirt with familiar, playful, and resonant piano trio dynamics. Arc No. 6 (to be released on October 10) “Momenta accumulate through return. Motion becomes practiced, framed by shared gravity and memory. Energy circulates without urgency, shaped by repetition and transformation. The past is present and future at once”. A further, urgent, cyclical rhythmic refinement is offered, faithfully captured in the short pieces “Arc” and “Dance”, shaped by nuanced repetitions and transformations. Arc No. 7 (to be released on November 9) “Time folds into itself. Multiple cycles coexist, asymmetrical yet connected. Movement breathes across layered durations, allowing contradiction to remain unresolved. The arc sustains density without weight, continuity without uniformity. Listening is wide enough to hold all the all of it”. Pendulum’s music plays a touch-and-go game in its own fragmented musical continuum, sustaining density without weight, continuity without uniformity, but with more structural focus. Arc No. 8 (to be released on December 9) “Strange tools reveal their logic through use. Motion disperses, leaving resonance rather than momentum. What remains feels everywhere at once, absorbed into space and attention. The arc settles without closing, as stillness carries the last trace of movement forward. It is the beginning of the end and the end of the beginning”. The concluding volume is not an end to this fascinating journey but a sort of beginning. The Pendulum trio already inhabited its own elastic conception of time, as the devoted listeners to this journey, and has established its idiosyncratic language. But Pendulum’s music tells us something deeper about life and the inevitable changes we experience throughout life. This trio asks us to adapt our time sensibility to its subtle transformations, fully embrace and be deeply attuned to our own ubiquitous cyclical and oscillating arcs, as we move forward, attempting to maintain an elusive balance. <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-1">Opening Arcs: Arc No. 1 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-2">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 2 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-3">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 3 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-4">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 4 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-5">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 5 by ILK</a > Email This BlogThis! items._cn_summary: 这是一支由法国钢琴家与丹麦低音提琴手、鼓手组成的钢琴三重奏，以'钟摆'为隐喻探索音乐中时间的多维度弹性。项目源自鼓手在丹麦皇家音乐学院发起的关于多时间运动与节奏设计的学术研究，计划在两年内以每月一卷的形式发布八张EP，总时长近三小时。乐队使用谱面与图形记谱结合的作曲片段，拒绝线性时间结构，让音乐以弧线或共享场域的方式展开。重音落在空间感、循环节奏位移与弹性乐句的编织上，文本强调深度聆听与耐心。作品中可见极简主义路径，如十七分钟的《Exercice Elastique》缓慢沉入脆弱而带有反叛意味的律动。整体呈现出学院气质浓厚的时间哲学实验，将即兴重力转化为摇摆节拍的全新可能。

items.body: Some promotion arrives generously late, but with this debut album by the Australian solo project Empty Vessel, I felt it was more than necessary to give it some attention anyway. Tom Wojcicki is an artist unknown to most, who released the album “Ruin Value” in the spring of 2025, an opus consisting of eight tracks. What I hear here defies all imagination: an absolute masterpiece in which the artist blends Industrial, Cinematic, and Ritual elements in a remarkably refined manner. He creates a tormented atmosphere of overwhelming sounds, with percussion effects that reverberate like drones. That overwhelming quality, in particular, is almost indescribable. Rarely have I encountered an artist capable of creating sounds as intense, present, and tormented as those of Empty Vessel. The tracks can be repetitive at times, but because of their sheer intensity, you are truly blown away. Before you know it, you are trapped in a sonic web of terrifying and illusory images. The album is a succession of insane tracks, meaning that you discover one highlight after another. If you are a fan of the genres mentioned above and are not yet familiar with Empty Vessel, I would simply recommend buying this album without listening to it beforehand. An absolute masterpiece, and it will not be easy to follow this up with an equally powerful successor. (Rating:9). Listen to “Scattered Pieces Of Her”: Scattered Pieces Of Her by Empty Vessel About Empty Vessel Empty Vessel is the solo industrial and power electronics project of Australian artist Tom Wojcicki. “Ruin Value” was released on 14 April 2025 through the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen as a hand-numbered CD limited to 200 copies with a 4-page booklet, plus a digital edition, under catalog number DP179CD. The album runs eight tracks, opening with “Scattered Pieces Of Her” and closing with “Zero Fetish”. Empty Vessel has also recorded under the names Droid Sector, Broken Fingers, Glass Barbeque, Aurora Seven and Cockroach Diocese. “Ruin Value” is Empty Vessel’s first release to be reviewed on Side-Line.
items._cn_summary: 澳大利亚单人项目Empty Vessel首张专辑《Ruin Value》由德国小厂牌Dunkelheit Produktionen发行，限量200张编号CD配四页册页。艺术家Tom Wojcicki将工业、电影化音景与仪式元素交织，以打击效果营造出类似无人机的持续共振，制造出强烈而扭曲的压迫氛围。整张专辑八首曲目彼此呼应，构成一张高密度的聆听体验：声响设计层次丰富，节奏虽具重复性，却以强度牵引听众深入。制作上不依赖旋律走向，而以质感与空间感取胜，低频厚重、噪音层堆叠紧凑，每一段都在构建听者无法轻易逃脱的声场。澳大利亚独立厂牌之外的小规模手工发行进一步凸显其地下属性，是暗潮与实验电子领域值得关注的作品。

items.body: " All Art Has Been Contemporary ” This sentence is a neon installation by conceptual artist Maurizio Nannucci located on the roof of the Galleria d'Arte Moderna in Torino, that takes up a similar concept expressed a few decades earlier by Pablo Picasso. Such a fundamental axiom, around which rivers of ink have been spilled, seems to lose its actualization in the late '70s, early '80s, with regard to jazz: this art form is out of sync with the “here and now” and doesn't dialogue with contemporary, ontologically expressed by young generations. Totally deprived of any chance to become aware of free/improv artists, the teens of the time (your humble writer among them) relate to jazz in the same way they approach Dante, Seneca or Milton in highschool or uni: respect, awe, in some cases sincere passion, more often distance. Wright or wrong, a matter of fact. Moreover, those years were destined to write one of the brightest chapters in the Great Book of Music, through amazing groups like Clock DVA, PIL, Joy Division, Talking Heads, Pere Ubu, X, Television, Bad Brains, Wire, just to throw out some names in bulk. Would it have made sense to spend the very little bucks in our pocket on Chet Baker instead of Meat Puppets and Husker Du? C’mon, a no-brainer. This inexhaustible cornucopia of punk/post-punk gems experiences a small, apparently insignificant, intermittence, which leads us, aboard the only ISO-certified Time Machine (the music), to where almost everything happens: New York. Here, while the ruins of CBGB's and Max's Kansas City are still smoking, a patrol of sappers (Contortions, Mars, DNA, Teenage Jesus and the Jerks), pushing far beyond punk, lights up the charges of the “No Wave”, generating a shockwave that transcends the scope of music and involves the most extremist artistic fringes of the East Village and the Lower East Side: poets (Lydia Lunch), writers (Kathy Acker), painters (Basquiat) and filmmakers (Eric Mitchell, Amos Poe) are up for It. Among them, relocated from Minnesota, John Lurie, iconic muse actor from Jim Jarmusch’s early movies, who in his unmissable autobiography, The History of Bones , offers us a snapshot of that sparkling, bohemian milieu: “We were so sure of ourselves, we never doubted anything. We were powerful, intelligent, energetic, confident, self-centered, and incredibly naive. Nothing outside our fourteen-block radius mattered. From Houston to 14th St., from the Bowery to Ave. A, that was the only universe.” John alternates between filmmaking and musical practicing, not on a third-hand Telecaster or on a battered Precision bass, but on alto saxophone: "At 4 p.m. on Main Street in Worcester, Massachusetts, the universe gave me my first saxophone. Nothing special happened, except that a man, driving around with a wheelbarrow, gave me a saxophone. I became like a monk. I slept on the floor, I didn't have a TV, I didn't smoke, I didn't drink, I didn't fuck. I played the saxophone until my fingers bled and I devoured music: Varese, Stravinsky, Mingus, Dolphy, Monk, Bird, Ornette, Hendrix." From there, it was a short step to form a band, and with his brother Evan on keyboards, the rhythm section of Steve Piccolo and Anton Fier (of Feelies “fame”), and the abrasive guitar of DNA’s Arto Lindsay (a very distinctive element of the ensemble), the Lounge Lizards were born, self-described, out of respect for the Masters of the Past, as "fake jazz." The Purists, losers by definition, take the bait and move on, while those with heart and soul stop, listen to and understand the new hybridization of tradition with the metro, iconoclastic, infectious, no-sounds: a sabotage of the “status quo ante” of jazz but, definitively, a Sabotage of Love. None of them graduated from Juilliard (does it matter?), but the Lizards' sound reflects like few others the zeitgeist of Downtown and the mood of those courageous and visionary prime movers who animate it. Their debut album was released in 1981, packaged with Peter Saville's splendid artwork, featuring a black-and-white photo of the musicians on the cover that always reminds us of Jimmy Giuffre's stunning "Free Fall". At the helm, the mighty Teo Macero who infuses the album with the nocturnal atmospheres that made it legendary, sitting the listener at the bar counter of Edward Hopper's "Nighthawks At Diner" or amidst a Raymond Chandler novel. The quick band’s development during the couple of years preceding it is captured on "Live 79-81," a reissue of the 1985 Roir cassette, containing live recordings at Hurrah and CBGB's in New York (June, August 1979), Her Majesty's Theater in London (June 1980), Cleveland Radio (June 1981), and Berlin Jazz Festival (December 1981). It's all there: contractions and swing, dissonances and post-post-bop, Earl Hagan (Harlem Nocturne) and Monk (Epistrophy), boredom and coolness, dark streets and streetlights. Jazz in its pure form. Did Lounge Lizards change the course of events? No. Did they spearhead a new musical stream? No. Did they contribute to ensuring that kids who grew up on punk could relate to jazz in an updated and conscious way? ABSOLUTELY YES. Same as it happened to John Lurie just some years before, then let him have the final words to come full circle: “When I was 17, someone made me listen to John Coltrane and it was as if he was speaking to me in Chinese. But how? Is there music I can't understand? And so I started listening to it all the time.” Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张现场录音合集收录了Lounge Lizards在1979至1981年间的演出，彼时纽约下城正处于No Wave运动的震荡之中。评论将乐队的诞生置于CBGB废墟与Max's Kansas City余烟之间的文化语境：朋克之后的极端主义从音乐蔓延至诗歌、绘画与电影，John Lurie以萨克斯而非吉他切入这片荒原。专辑记录了Lounge Lizards作为No Wave景观中独特一支的现场面貌——他们既不属于纯粹的自由即兴，也未彻底投入后朋克的工业喧嚣，而是以爵士乐器在极简主义与粗粝噪声之间寻找张力。评论追溯了Lurie从明尼苏达移居纽约后融入东村艺术圈的经历，强调这群艺术家以十四个街区为宇宙的偏执与自信。录音本身呈现出早期No Wave爵士乐现场罕见的原始能量与结构纪律并存的状态。

items.body: Josh Mason’s L+ marks the second to last release for the Dauw label for 2018. In the ‘About’ section of his website, Mason talks about working ‘ in different processing environments’ and although he is talking about the tools to make the sounds, Mason’s compositions in L+ do feel like he is creating environments for his melodies to inhabit. L+ opens into existence with a modulated sound, slowly undulating. Quickly from that single sound branches off three or four strands of sound that are then drawn back into it, to be re-immersed. But that core sound that brought the piece still lives on, underneath it all. And this is where the notion of creating audio environments is a useful lens to view L+’s compositions – it’s as if Mason is defining the piece of land or territory where his sonic strands will live. And this is one of the repeated techniques on L+: most pieces start with a sound that remains the foundation for the duration of the piece. Also typical of L+ is those sonic/musical strands that exist on or against the backdrop of sonic land that Mason creates for each composition. They often present themselves as glitches – microcosms of sound – that simply burst into existence and move along. None of those strands of sound really comes together, but nothing really runs counter to any of the other sounds at play. It’s as if Mason sends his players in motion but bounds them – they can go where they may and interact as they will, but they all exist within a sort of fenced-in confines. And the real magic is in the way those strands overlay or inhabit the space of that core sound upon which they exist. Across the 6 pieces of L+ Mason plays with that formula and, interestingly, L+ almost becomes more minimal as it proceeds. It’s as if by slowing things down, yes, things sound a little glitchier and we are closer to the mechanics of the compositions, and still, somehow, they become more immersive. In some cases, the composition’s move so slow, those strands of sound almost literally sound like electricity moving across a a wire. Of the album Mason writes: “I had seneca’s letters on ethics and epictetus’ enchiridion right next to me. as i considered the choices i was making with the sounds you hear, i was also pausing to have a think on the things i was reading. each track corresponds with some maxim found in either copy i had of each book (ie S26 = seneca, pg. 26.) the first piece and last piece are based on a two part axiom, and so both pieces are connected sonically in some ways, as two ends of a piece of tape might be spliced together.” Ambient/minimal electronic music as philosophy is interesting territory because there is something to be said for the broad philosophy that ambient music asks us to slow down in an ever quickening world. But what Mason is talking about is a bit different, in that he is taking the treatises and tracts of other thinkers and basing his sounds around their ideas to create sound explorations or meditations of their philosophies and put those ideas into sonic motion. My first note when starting to write my review of L+ was to write “ Can an album be welcoming without first being inviting?”. The coarse aspects of those glitchy components seemed, objectively speaking, abrasive – even against their seemingly subdued backdrops. But, once immersed, everything about L+ feels full and, yes, inviting even. In the world of L+ sounds pop, crackle, hiss, undulate, vibrate, wave, disintegrate, flicker, and feel sometimes random, but there is no entropy – there are entire worlds at play in each composition. L+ is a sublime collection of minimal electronic music that nicely wraps up 2018. L+ by Josh Mason www.dauw.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: Josh Mason的专辑L+由Dauw厂牌发行，作品以单一核心音色为基础搭建声音环境，在此基础上衍生出多线索的声响碎片，如同在特定区域内活动的声音群落。六首曲目沿用此公式，但随着推进呈现逐步极简化的趋势，慢速运动中的碎片音色愈发接近电流沿导线传递的质感。Mason以斯多葛学派塞涅卡与爱比克泰德的伦理学著作为创作参照，每首曲目对应书中某一格言，首尾两曲在声音上形成呼应。整体作品将氛围音乐视为哲学冥想的载体，在处理声音选择的同时阅读古代文本，使听觉体验与思想探索同步展开，构成一种以极简电子手法承载文本思辨的实验性创作路径。

items.body: “I was interested in distress sounds, sirens, flares, etc,” reads a peculiar passage from the press junket for Jake Marshall’s debut album. Quite humorously, the same statement could double as surplus copy for Her Majesty’s Coastguard. The London-based musician and visual artist’s exploratory first release, Fresh Water, features eight tracks themed around motifs of emergency and crisis. With a conceptual arc starring repurposed survival signals, one might forecast a cyclone worthy of striking scurvy into the heartiest sea-wizened veteran. Instead, Marshall’s Fresh Water thrills with rhythmic revelations, inducing sonic mirages along the way. Whether shipwrecked or just plain lost, survival calls have served a single purpose throughout history: When facing threat to life or limb, one must make a visible or audible signal which will draw immediate attention. Quite tellingly, blaring alarms initiate Fresh Water: a quartet of sirens sizzle in mid- and hi-frequencies throughout “P5ws.” Woven together sparingly, frayed horns pulse in binary hysteria as synthetic strings shudder beneath. Directed by a drum beat ricocheting down dub hallways, “Forgo” bristles with elongated notes trembling in monotone to the image of a lonely flare sinking slowly underwater. Looped into modulated motifs akin to a minimalist composer with an ear for Krautrock, the sirens return on “Grid,” ear-piercing and chest-rattling, throbbing for spine-tingling miles. “Jan 1” opens with a celestial transmission: squelching feedback spins in limbo across ham radio frequencies; ghostly harmonics arouse the stereo field to a mild melody light enough to catch a breeze—or a cold. “Thro” ignites its twilight signal on the deck of the stranded cargo ship. But the search boat’s probing lights sweep right by, oblivious to the blazing oil barrel shrouded by fog. Now try to get some sleep. Fatigue setting in, Fresh Water’s title track revives the remaining survivors with club-ready sirens. Cycling up and down frenetic scales, white light from a high intensity strobe machine pulses vigorously on a dance floor driven by 4/4 beats. Cast in the nimbus of neon glow sticks, the mid-track lull blurs into an elfin trill: woozy like a Wurlitzer high on helium. A fluttering flute descends, fending off flies: wah-wah’d notes washed by an oblivion of pitch-shifted keys. As the helicopters circle nearby, keep both arms outstretched—raising and lowering them repeatedly. “Like A Mothers Love” exudes little assurance in said patrimonial affection. A vaguely Middle-Eastern melody pushes through static, liquefying into the skipping bass of a fog horn. Other accoutrements gradually festoon the proceedings: a sonic ritual forms around the raising of a maritime flag; hollow synths float steadily behind a constellation of electronic clamoring; a bobbing bass line, punctuated by hollow wood blocks, carries a Morse code transmission into heat-craze and hunger. Apply sunscreen liberally. “Outro” introduces resignation onto the lone life raft. Ruffled waves nudge the rubber boat sideways, the microphone crackling with an indifferent wind. As the stranded oil tanker slumps into the water: cavernous explosions boom alongside handguns fired overhead. A solemn synth tapers towards blackout, reaching for rations and reasons. Leery that the nearing helicopter may be merely a hallucination, the sole survivor casts dye markers overboard—just to be safe. The search team hovers on the horizon as lazy waves guide a pool of green dye starboard: drifting away from the raft, pulling towards a final hope. Although not without aquatic dangers, Fresh Water graciously negates the possibility of death by drowning or predation. Playfully buoyant and brightly colored, there is no need to measure Fresh Water’s salinity. And yet the absence of salt is no guarantee that sun or wave might not still maim. When sailing through Fresh Water, make sure to pack those suede shoes with a polyester vest. Only cinch the life jacket snugly, and hurl the preserver wide when Jake Marshall is on duty. items._cn_summary: Jake Marshall首张专辑以求救信号、警报器与烟雾弹为核心概念素材，将八首作品串联成一个完整的海上求生叙事弧线。音乐采用极简主义循环结构与Krautrock式的调制动机，警报声被拆解为高、中频段的嘶鸣与脉冲，在立体声场中编织成断续的节奏网络。合成弦乐在dub式鼓点下颤抖延伸，幽灵般的谐波在中东风格旋律中液化，与雾号低音交织成频段对话。木块敲击传递摩斯密码般的电子信号，Wurlitzer键盘与哇音长笛交替出现，营造出从迷幻恍惚到俱乐部节拍的跨度。整体声音设计兼具环境氛围的沉浸感与节奏张力，把危机主题转化为一种结构化的听觉探索。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,

Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 携重组项目 United States of Alchemy 回归，联合前卫作曲家 Paladino 与诗人 Ferrari 推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》。十一首歌曲以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管、合成器泛音与金属质感音色，构成非线性的模态化音景，挑战西方听众对和声进行的固有认知。Moskowitz 苍老而充满阅历的嗓音承载哲学化歌词，旋律如意识流般起伏，不遵循传统调性逻辑，而是让每个词都获得充分的音乐重量。歌词延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统，《Pale Wanderer》直指专制主义的帮凶机制，《Charlottesville》以与已故 Joe Byrd 合作的方式揭露白人至上主义的种族净化话语，同时也有对死亡与宇宙位置的沉思。整体呈现出高远而真诚的政治意识与艺术追求。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴厅完成了一场两小时的独奏即兴录制，后经后期混音加入人声采样、打击乐、循环段落、田野录音及偶然声响。整张专辑呈现冥想式的创作状态，与萨沙格里琴般的低音脉动、喉音泛音的禅意遥相呼应。Sosa 拒绝被风格归类，融合爵士、拉美、古典与电子元素，强调首遍录音的即兴自然性。专辑在空旷音乐厅中录制，捕捉到钢琴的完整共鸣与泛音层次，声音处理保留了内在探索的质感。跨界即兴与世界音乐元素结合，制作手法兼具实验性与文化深度。

items.body: A centuries-old devotional song from Morocco’s Gnawa repertoire, “M’Bara Meskin” tells of poor M’Bara, left outside the shrine in torn clothes to brew his tea from leaves others have thrown away. Inside, the Sidi and the Lalla, Moroccan honorifics for a gentleman and a lady, sip theirs in their slippers. Sydney-born multi-instrumentalist Julian Belbachir has rebuilt it on reggae and dub, keeping the vocal in Moroccan Arabic, from sessions in Morocco, Mali, Australia, Canada and Jamaica. Belbachir was born to a Moroccan father and an Australian mother and grew up in Surry Hills and Redfern, where he started on West African drums at five under griots and master drummers from Sydney’s African diaspora. He went on to study percussion and instrument-making in Guinea, Senegal, Mali and Morocco, and plays the kamele n’goni, the harp-lute of Mali’s Wassoulou region. From 2013 to 2022 he drummed for the Australian Indigenous dub band OKA, and after the death of its founder, Stuart “Boga” Fergie, he went solo with his 2022 debut album, Babdoukkala. Gnawa music was carried into Morocco by West Africans brought north across the Sahara, many of them enslaved, and the personnel on his forthcoming album, The Golden Light, follow the same route: more than 30 musicians from Mali and Morocco, among them Moussa Diakite, lead guitarist for Salif Keita. “M’Bara Meskin” came out on 11 September as its first single, with the album due in February 2027. Belbachir hears the song as a portrait of “the hardships musicians face in their daily lives“. The video, shot on Super 8 over two trips to Essaouira three years apart, follows his collaborators through rehearsals, recording sessions and time with their community in the Atlantic port best known for its annual Gnawa festival. items._cn_summary: Julian Belbachir 是一位出生于悉尼的摩洛哥裔多乐器演奏家，他将一首有数百年历史的摩洛哥 Gnawa 宗教歌曲重建于雷鬼与 dub 的律动之上，保留了阿拉伯语人声。歌曲讲述了贫穷的 M'Bara 被留在神庙外、用他人丢弃的茶叶煮茶的故事，Belbachir 将其理解为音乐人日常艰辛的写照。新专辑《The Golden Light》由来自摩洛哥、马里等地的三十多位音乐人合作录制，参与者包括 Salif Keita 的首席吉他手 Moussa Diakite，制作跨越摩洛哥、马里、澳大利亚、加拿大与牙买加等多地。Belbachir 早年随非洲 diaspora 鼓师学习，后在几内亚、塞内加尔、马里与摩洛加研习打击乐与乐器制作，并演奏马里 Wassoulou 地区的竖琴琴 kamele n'goni。音乐录像以 Super 8 胶片在大西洋港口 Essaouira 拍摄，记录了排练、录音与社区生活。该作品体现了跨撒哈拉迁徙路线在当代音乐中的延续。

items.body: The German duo Grimoire De Occulte has been active for several years now and has released the majority of its work, particularly in recent years. Inspired by Bernd Hermanns, aka ‘Baal’ (owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen and also active in several other projects), and ‘Philosoph’, they originally released this album in 2025, with the CD version following this year. The title word ‘Ajna’ undoubtedly refers to the Sanskrit word usually translated as ‘perceiving’, ‘knowing’, or ‘insight’. It also represents the sixth chakra, which is associated with the so-called third eye. This aligns perfectly with the approach of this project, which has always been closely linked to ritual and mysticism. We are presented with an elaborate and unique track lasting nearly 40 minutes. “Ajna: Transmissions” invites the listener to immerse themselves in an esoteric world in which the ‘other side’ plays a prominent role. This naturally provides inspiration for a dark composition, with the duo presenting us with a persistent, ominous wave of sound. At first glance, it may seem somewhat monotonous, yet the composition is enriched with humming sound effects and additional sounds, including all kinds of crackling field recordings. The whole piece is also punctuated by a scream, which adds extra power to the dark ritual. As far as I’m concerned, a few additional tracks could have been included here, but this extended “Ajna: Transmissions” remains a pleasant listen nonetheless. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Anja: Transmissions”: https://dunkelheitprod.bandcamp.com/track/ajna-transmissions
items._cn_summary: 德国二人组 Grimoire De Occulte 发行专辑《Ajna: Transmissions》，标题源自梵语，关联第六脉轮与第三眼意象，延续了项目一贯的神秘仪式主题。整张专辑仅由一首近四十分钟的长篇作品构成，以持续不断的暗色音浪为骨架，叠加蜂鸣音效与大量噼啪作响的田野录音，并在中段插入一声尖叫以强化仪式感。整体编排偏向环境与无人机手法，节奏变化有限但通过声音层次的逐渐堆积营造出沉浸式的黑暗氛围。由于仅有一首曲目，乐评人认为若能增加更多短篇作品则结构会更完整，但作为单段冥想式的聆听体验仍属合格之作。

items.body: Fawning, we’re brighter, we’re cautious, Falling like fighters, we’re caustic. Cracked up like actors, we’re lying. Daydreams and nightmares. Sharing cigarettes and leather trousers can feel like a promising start to eternity, until eternity begins to resemble an argument neither person can leave. Berlin’s Night Nail take that unhappy prospect to the dance floor on Vile Train, a gothic rock seduction in which two lovers become so absorbed in each other that escape begins to seem as impossible as happiness. The attraction is considerable; so is the damage. The song previews Infinite Fountain, Night Nail’s fourth studio album, due November 6, 2026, through Icy Cold Records. Its accompanying video reunites the band with director and editor Jean De Oliviera, whose previous collaborations include Hollow Day, Little Armenia, and Narcoleptic Dream Catcher. Vile Train begins with a noise suspended somewhere between a buzz and a screech, while cold guitar tones gather around it with considerable menace. The drums establish their footing before a heavier, sustained riff saws through the opening, its melody making the abrasion strangely inviting. Around the thirty-second mark, the bass enters with a deep, brooding groove, and the guitar shifts into a lower, more resonant register. That change gives the song a mournful richness, setting the scene for Brandon Robert’s dark, swaggering delivery. Repeating synth figures tighten the tension beneath his voice, and roughly a minute in, the chorus sends the arrangement into a more urgent gothic dance beat. The construction is remarkably assured: each entrance increases the pressure, while the bass keeps enough melodic independence to make the groove feel alive. By the three-minute mark, its intricate phrasing has become a hook in its own right, moving beneath Robert’s breathy repetition of “Daydreams and nightmares” as a feminine voice echoes the words in whispers. The song’s pleasure comes from those relationships between the instruments, the way an ominous opening develops into something so physically persuasive. Robert found the initial inspiration during a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested a romance with a particularly poor prognosis. In the song’s conception, two dreamers inhabit separate modern realities until their fantasies bring them together. They exchange clothes, cigarettes, and intimacies, gradually making a prison of the connection that first seemed to offer freedom. Robert describes the result as “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The lyrics give that deterioration a nasty intimacy. Caution sits beside fawning, attraction beside aggression, and the lovers seem increasingly aware of the roles they have been playing. “Some days I wish I was her” carries the confusion further, towards the point where wanting another person begins to erase the distinction between their identity and your own. Against the recurring admission of lies, the fantasy of America offers another possible elsewhere. Every imagined exit seems to lead back to the same two people. Vile Train was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. That combination serves a song whose writing and arrangement make its gothic excess feel earned, with a chorus capable of turning private misery into a crowded dance floor. Directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera, the video gives Vile Train a stark black-and-white treatment, cutting between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor shots framed by stone arches and fountain basins. Black leather, dark glasses, and severe makeup give the pair a suitably funereal glamour, while tight shots of fingers on strings bring the song’s instrumental interplay into focus. Robert’s face repeatedly fills the frame, his dark lipstick and pale features isolated against the black background. Grain, scratches, and superimposed silhouettes of reaching hands disturb that severe simplicity, spreading across faces and instruments until the musicians seem caught behind the image itself. Robert’s own gestures towards the lens make the camera feel uncomfortably close, turning performance into something between an invitation and an accusation. The recurring close-ups and grasping hands give the song’s obsession a physical form, suggesting an intimacy that has become impossible to escape. It is an effective visual rendering of what the band calls the “afterlife of relationship hell,” where the desire to hold someone close has acquired a distinctly claustrophobic meaning. Watch the video for Vile Train below: Formed in Los Angeles in 2013, Night Nail relocated to Berlin in 2018, the year their debut album LA Demons appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed through Cold Transmission in 2020, with Fates Explained arriving on Metropolis Records in 2023. The archival release Early Demons and Demos and remix album Fates Remade followed in 2024. Their earlier work with producer Pete Burns of Kill Shelter helped establish a catalogue that connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes. Infinite Fountain also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the album with shows across the US, UK, and Europe during 2026–2027. In the meantime, explore their back catalog on Bandcamp. Follow Night Nail: Bandcamp Spotify Facebook Instagram YouTube Website The post “Daydreams and Nightmares” — Night Nail Turns Desire Into Damnation in Video for “Vile Train” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Night Nail来自柏林，这首《Vile Train》作为第四张专辑《Infinite Fountain》的先行单曲，融合了哥特摇滚与后朋克的舞蹈化节拍。歌曲以嗡鸣与尖锐噪音开场，冷色调吉他层层叠加，贝斯在三十秒处进入深沉律动，与主唱Brandon Robert暗沉的吟唱形成张力。副歌部分切入更急促的哥特舞蹈节奏，合成器持续制造压迫感，器乐间的关系构成核心听觉趣味。创作灵感源于庞贝古城一幅描绘天使与恶魔相拥的壁画，两人在现代现实中相遇，交换衣物与亲密感，却在最初看似自由的连接中逐渐构筑牢笼。歌词中自我与他者身份的消融成为核心意象，作品以扭曲而美的方式探讨爱的黑暗真相，展现了类型框架内相当成熟的编曲控制力。

items.album: Faded Pulse Finds Solace in the Past on Ethereal Goth Album “Elysia”

items.body: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry and Victorian painting. Acoustic guitars, hammered dulcimer, electric bass, and ambient synthesizers accompany water spirits, waiting maidens, and woodland gatherings whose hosts have questionable intentions. The route here runs through the synthpop of 2025’s Submission and the more ethereal leanings of that year’s Fallen EP, with a decisive turn taken while watching Monica Richards perform with Strange Boutique in Washington. Johnson’s affection for the 1990s Projekt catalogue supplies another set of coordinates: Lycia, Love Spirals Downwards, Black Tape for a Blue Girl, and Unto Ashes sit alongside the folk of Pentangle and Donovan. There is a generous curiosity at work, the kind that can find room for both a Slowdive bassline and a William Morris poem without making either feel like an unlikely guest. Johnson’s background in art history gives Elysia a visual life as rich as its musical references. Waterhouse’s paintings, the Arts and Crafts movement, and Art Nouveau belong to the same imaginative world as thrifted velvet, medieval dress, and an old copy of Tennyson found in an antique shop. Beneath the finery lie practical questions about courage, community, and how to remain attentive to the living world. This gathering of fairies may be perilous, but the hope is that listeners return from it with a renewed appetite for their own lives. We spoke with Johnson about the records that opened those doors, the literature and paintings behind Elysia, and the enduring possibilities of ethereal music, from a hammered dulcimer to a dream performance among the art and architecture of the Cloisters. Before Faded Pulse, what first opened the door to the Gothic imagination for you? Was there a particular record, book, painting, or encounter that made you feel you had found somewhere you belonged? Faded Pulse: I started getting into the gothic scene when I was around 14 years old, and at that time my most essential record was The Cure’s Pornography. I loved the dense, almost psychedelic sound of the album. I’ve probably overplayed that record way too much at that age. Yet it really cemented my love for atmosphere and dense sound design. Robert Smith’s honest and vulnerable lyricism made me feel so seen and got me through so much. Between Submission, Fallen, and Elysia, your music has moved further into folk and ethereal wave. What was happening in your life and listening habits that encouraged that change, and what could you express through these arrangements that you hadn’t explored before? Faded Pulse: When I first started “Submission” around 2022, I was very much into the New Wave and Synthpop sounds of the 80s, and that really shows on that album, although my listening has always been more eclectic. One big influence on Elysia was psych and folk of the 60s and 70s, particularly bands like Pentangle; their album Solomon’s Seal was super influential on me, especially songs like “Willy O’Winsbury”. Donovan was another big influence; you can really hear it on songs like “Will Thy Heart Be True,” where I go for a more folky, ballad-type song. I have always had a huge love for the 90’s ethereal scene. The moment I knew I wanted to move sonically towards that was when I saw Strange Boutique live at the Black Cat in D.C. in 2025. Seeing Monica Richards on stage and hearing the music live was really a light-bulb moment for me. Ethereal allows me to experiment more with unusual instrumentation and also lets the music take people to another world. Although I enjoyed making synth pop, here I can play with classical, folk, ambient, and even more rock-oriented structures. It’s so much more playful and freeing. I feel like Faded Pulse would have been a perfect fit for Projekt Festival, especially the 1997 edition. How were you first introduced to the label and its artists, and was there a particular band or record that sparked your affinity for that strain of ethereal music? Faded Pulse: Projekt has a special place in my heart and is probably one of my favorite labels ever. My essential four artists from the record label are Black Tape, Lycia, Love Spirals, and Unto Ashes. Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” is one of my all-time favs; it is a masterpiece in its own right in sound design and atmosphere, and it’s both deeply haunting and romantic. I feel like Love Spirals Downwards Idylls is glaringly obvious as one of the influences on Elysia, and I feel it is their most essential record. It’s hard for me to choose a Lycia album because they’re my favorite band on the label, but if I had to choose, it would be “A Day in the Stark Corner”. It’s equal parts dreamy, cold, and bleak. Unto Ashes serves everything I look for in a band: medieval instruments and sounds, folk and darkwave synths. I feel like their album “Empty into white” is so sonically rich and put together, sinister yet dreamy. I’m not sure how I even stumbled on the label, which feels fitting, like it came to me almost in a dream; it is the most influential group of artists for me. There’s something about Elysia that feels entirely at home in the pages of Propaganda or Carpe Noctem. What feels special to you about the Gothic culture of the ’90s, and how have you encountered that period through its music, magazines, photography, and fashion? Faded Pulse: Funnily enough, I own an issue of Propaganda, No. 22, and I wanna say it’s from 1994-1996. I have very fond memories of reading Propaganda magazines in high school on the Internet Archive. I am a historian at heart and love to learn everything I can about culture, music, and fashions of any time period I study. The 90’s, to me, feel somehow criminally underrated, even though it was when the gothic scene was at its peak and fully found itself and diversified into many different interests. I feel the worship of the 80s has caused people to overlook how creative the scene was in the 90s. Even now, somehow darkwave from the 90s is still more experimental and fresh than the very 80s-oriented sounds we get today. As for the fashion, I would study a lot of the pictures on Pinterest from magazines, club shoots, or people’s personal uploads, and when I went thrifting, I would look for similar items. PVC, Satins, Silks, and Velvet are all mainstays in my closet thanks to the 90s, haha. “Meadow of My Mind” and “Upon the Heavens” feel like a bridge between Cocteau Twins and the more romantic corners of the Projekt catalogue. How do you approach the relationship between voice and guitar in these songs, especially when both seem capable of carrying the melody or dissolving into one another? Faded Pulse: Much like the bands before me, I kind of treat the voice as just another instrument. When recording a lot of these songs, I wanted the guitar and voice to mesh well. In meadow of my mind, the voice and guitar switch throughout the song, giving them space to drive the song along without clashing. In “Meadow of My Mind,” you sing, “Leave this dying world behind,” yet you’ve described Elysia as something beyond escapism. What does that inner refuge make possible for you, and what do you hope listeners bring back from it into their everyday lives? Faded Pulse: To me, “Meadow of my Mind” is about the love of nature, to put it plainly. When listeners “Leave the realm of Elysia,” I want people to bring that sort of magic into their everyday lives. Whether that be getting involved in their local communities, making art, or reading poetry. Whatever it is that makes you feel connected to the world around you. “Upon the Heavens” uses the language of prayer, reaching toward a divine presence and asking to be heard and healed. What is your relationship with that devotional language, and how did you arrive at the kind of sacred experience you wanted the song to convey? Faded Pulse: To me, music is very spiritual, and I definitely wanted Upon the Heavens to emulate that in some way. It’s not a song devoted to a particular deity or religion, but it is about reaching out and feeling something greater. I feel this all the time through music, when I listen to a song that just makes me float away or feel high on euphoria. I mean, historically speaking, music is how people connect to the otherworld and is used in ritual, even though it is now far removed from its sacred roots. Music still feels deeply spiritual and otherworldly, and I think that’s truly what the song conveys. “Lamia’s Kiss” brings to mind Dead Can Dance’s exploration of musical traditions beyond rock, with an experimental quality that feels ancient and unfamiliar at once. Which specific traditions, recordings, or instruments informed it, and how did you develop its musical character? Faded Pulse: The sounds of the Middle East and the Mediterranean very much inspire Lamia’s kiss. A lot of the bands I liked, like Lovespirals, DCD, and Rajna, had eastern influence in their music, so it kinda bled into my consciousness. Rather than writing cliched lyrics about her as a figure, I wanted the song to emulate what it would feel like to be caught in her hypnotic gaze, to be pulled in. Instrumentally, I wanted the Dulcimer to be the lead on the song, which I feel really harnesses that archaic, almost ancient vibe that I wanted the song to have. I also grew up in Asia for a short time. I do think it had a musical effect on me, and it seems only natural that an experience like that would creep into my music in some way. What first drew you to Lamia as a figure? Did you come to her through mythology, Keats’s poem, a painting, or another interpretation, and what interests you about the meeting of beauty, desire, and danger in her story? Faded Pulse: It’s a little bit of all of that. Keats’s poem is definitely an inspo, as is Waterhouse’s iconic painting. I am also a Lilith and Hecate Devotee; the lamia is associated with both, so it’s almost devotional. I also love serpentine imagery and symbolism, as well as the figure of the femme fatale, so it is essentially a collage of many different ideas and feelings. “Fair Lady in Gold” has a baroque richness and a medieval atmosphere, particularly in the bright, struck-string sound that suggests a hammered dulcimer. How did you build that arrangement, and who—or what—is the lady at its center? Faded Pulse: For “Fair Lady in Gold,” I knew I wanted to have a few instrumental tracks on the album. The main instruments here are my Dusty Strings hammered dulcimer and my Korg Minilogue for ambient synths. There is no single song as an influence; rather, months and weeks of studying and listening to music from the Renaissance and medieval period that shaped this song. When I first started writing “The Lady in Gold,” I was envisioning Cordelia from King Lear in a painting by Edwin Austin Abbey. Although her gown is yellow, it is not even close to gold, haha. However, a woman with a golden pooling Bliaut gown was what I was envisioning when creating the song, so the name kinda stuck. “Summerland” seems to occupy a meeting place between Dead Can Dance and Cocteau Twins, while its lyrics describe being drawn into a fairy gathering. How welcoming did you want that invitation to feel, and how much uncertainty or danger belongs within its beauty? Faded Pulse: Summerland is definitely a song where I wanted the listener to be taken away by the fae, where it’s both exhilarating and panic-inducing. To be led away and dancing with beings who look human, yet there is something quite off about them, and strange things happen around them. I wanted to evoke the same feelings I had reading Irish fairy tales, where the stories of the fae are both wondrous and terrifying in equal measure. I think it’s a great metaphor for nature itself. Beautiful yet dangerous. “Undine” recalls the dreamier side of 4AD, alongside Faith and the Muse and Lycia, but its bassline and guitar flourishes also make ethereal wave’s goth and post-punk origins audible. How conscious are you of that connection when writing, and what does the bass allow you to do beneath such expansive arrangements? Faded Pulse: The bassline for Undine was heavily inspired by the bassline in Slowdive’s “Ballad of Sister Sue.” I knew I wanted this waltzy song where the bass carried much of the song’s sway. To me, the bass here is the most important; it just wouldn’t sound the same with a synth bass. It really gives the song that romantic rhythm I feel it needed. The words to “Undine” address the water-born figure directly, questioning her lover’s constancy and encouraging her to voice her feelings. Whose voice did you imagine addressing her, and what did you want your interpretation to reveal about her beyond the familiar tragedy? Faded Pulse: With Undine, I knew I really wanted to do a melancholic song about a siren, where the song itself is almost like a lament, where it feels like a spell is being cast onto the listener. The voice that carries the song is part third-person narrator and part Undine’s voice. The Chorus is nonsensical and is a made-up language, but it is Undine casting her spell, hoping and praying to keep Huldbrand’s love. The third-person voice beckons Undine to own her sadness and heartbreak to sing what’s in her heart and drown in her tears, tragically ending the knight’s life, but also having the strength to embrace her own emotions of love and betrayal. “Will Thy Heart Be True?” has the feel of an ethereal folk ballad, with its knight, waiting maiden, and tests of courage. Which Arthurian or medieval texts informed the song, and what does the question of remaining true mean to you personally? Faded Pulse: I think the concept of knight and maiden came to me through William Morris’s poem “Two Red Roses Across the Moon.” Although I’ve been a fan of Morris for a few years, I first heard of it when I visited the American Arts and Crafts Museum and saw a mural depicting the maiden from the poem waiting for her knight, who was off at war. Although I love the stereotypical depiction of the medieval romance trope, the song really isn’t solely about that. It is about staying strong during dark times and finding the courage to go on, which I feel is extremely relevant. Now, the question “Will Thy Heart be True?” is really asking, “Do you have the strength to keep fighting the good fight?” even when it seems hopeless. Your influences include Romantic literature, medieval poetry, and Victorian fairy tales. Which writers have most shaped your imagination—Keats, Christina Rossetti, William Morris, or perhaps someone less immediately expected? Could you take us through one passage or story that found its way into Elysia? Faded Pulse: One of my biggest influences was Alfred Lord Tennyson’s Idylls of the King, a book I thrifted in an antique shop. It features a poetic retelling of Arthurian legends, and although none of its stories made it into Elysia, I knew I wanted Elysia to evoke the feeling of magic, mystery, and romance that the book gave me. Poems like Coleridge’s Christabel and Keats’s La Belle Dame sans Merci were hugely influential as well. Keats’s story of the Faery woman leading the gullible knight astray was definitely an inspo for Summerland. Your art-history background brings the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau, and the Arts and Crafts movement into the album’s conception. Is there a particular work by an artist such as Burne-Jones, Waterhouse, or Mucha that you could place beside one of these songs and explain the connection? Faded Pulse: Rather than a single painting, artwork, or artist, Elysia sounds like the movements as a whole and what they were trying to achieve. To me, I want people to look at any art from any of those movements and instantly think of a song from Elysia. But if I had to choose an image to associate with the album, I would choose Waterhouse’s Ophelia, as it was one of the few paintings that made me think, “I want to make music that emulates how this painting feels.” Your photographs feature flowing robes, a circlet, a sword, woodland, and Gothic architecture. Which historical garments, designers, films, or figures inform your sense of dress, and how much of that appearance comes from making or adapting things yourself? Faded Pulse: A lot of Elysia’s costumes are based on a combination of different things. For me, it was studying fashion history throughout the Middle Ages, a lot of the Medieval revival clothing coming out of the goth scene in the 90s, and of course, fantasy films like The Lord of the Rings (Particularly the elves). Photographs of Lisa Hammer and Monica Richards in the 90s and 00s were also influential on me. To me, Lisa is a modern Pre-Raphaelite fashion icon, and I definitely wanted to emulate that for Elysia. A lot of the wardrobe for the photos was thrifted or modified to achieve that vibe. What do you think made ethereal wave such a natural home for medieval romance, folklore, and mystery? Within your own music, what do those older forms of imagination allow you to say about love, longing, or belonging in the present? Faded Pulse: I think there’s something very classic about medieval folklore and stories. They feel very timeless with their usage of romance, bravery, and fighting for something you think is worth fighting for. They capture what it means to be human and to be alive. I think Medieval and Ethereal are so drawn to each other because they both have a sense of whimsy and otherworldliness. I think this element of fantasy is so unique to Ethereal outside of the other core genres of the gothic scene. With ethereal, I can weave stories and ambiance that fully immerse the listener into the world I want to create, and I think that’s why fairytales and ethereal go so well together; it’s a perfect mesh of storytelling and sonic immersion. An enduring part of the Gothic imagination is its embrace of mystery and the wonders of nature. Do you feel that connection is more important than ever in this age of AI, and what role can music play in keeping that sense of wonder alive? Faded Pulse: I think music is more important now than ever in the age of AI. It requires you to engage no matter what, to let go, sit down, and spend your time listening, to feel something. I think music is intrinsically human, and I feel that when people go out to clubs or venues for shows and connect with those around them, it really helps them disconnect from the haze of being online all the time and brings them into the present. There is something magical about watching people perform and bring something out of you. That is something that AI could never replace. If you could present Elysia in a setting entirely of your choosing, what would a Faded Pulse performance look and feel like? How would the space, clothing, and instrumentation help bring listeners into these songs, and what would you want them to feel when they stepped outside again? Faded Pulse: I think two of my dream performance locations would be a medieval ruin or within the Met Cloisters Museum in New York. I feel like being surrounded by actual medieval art and architecture would really set the ambiance. One thing I’ve heard of is that bands in the 90s would have incense burning on stage. I don’t know how true that is, and of course, venues would never allow that now, but I think something like frankincense or sandalwood would be my chosen scent, and I feel like playing with multiple senses would really elevate the performance. For dress, I think it would be cool to have a lot of the new-agey medieval revival looks from the nineties that were popular in the scene, and, of course, I would encourage everyone to participate in dressing up if they so choose. For me, I want the audience to feel like they entered another realm, dreamy and untethered, and when they leave, feeling like they had a spiritual awakening.§ For all its mythic tales of knights, faeries, and enchanted waters, Elysia is an album that keeps returning to the ordinary work of being present: listening closely, making something, finding courage, and spending time with other people. Johnson’s ideal audience might gather in velvet beneath medieval arches, but the invitation extends well beyond that imagined evening. There is room for wonder in a borrowed book, a local show, or an afternoon among the trees, and Faded Pulse offers plenty of reasons to make room for it. Faded Pulse’s Elysia is out now. Listen to the album below and order here. items.album: Tony Njoku ~ A World of Bodies on Fire
items.excerpt: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music.
