items.body: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music. The title track establishes the EP’s sound through layers of synthesiser harmonies that gather pace but stop short of a conventional climax. “Streams and Storms” turns towards private reflection, while “The Quiet Chaos of Playing It Safe” holds onto its tension without seeking a dramatic release. “Etude No. 1” strips the music down again, bringing the record to a sombre close. As Njoku explains in the accompanying interview, his move away from language is connected to an interest in how music can communicate feelings before they have been organised into words. Grief, exhaustion and recovery remain unresolved, expressed through harmony, resonance, dynamics and space. Small harmonic changes assume greater significance within these sparse arrangements. This is no suite in four movements, with constrasting character and same key signature. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE is a protean EP that searches and digs inwards, taking unexpected turns without any desire to dazzle. There is no show-off moment, no virtuoso display demanding attention, nor any grand moment of portending grief; emotion remains understated and kept in check. The music is unafraid of intimacy, allowing sustained harmonies, shifts in density and silence to determine its course, leaving much of the experience behind these compositions unspoken. To help us put out the fire we reached out directly to Tony Njoku for an interview conducted via email. All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was a large-scale collaborative statement concerned with spiritual preparedness, cultural resistance and collective survival, while the Bloom releases increasingly embraced instrumental composition, chamber arrangements and themes of grief, memory and renewal. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels like a further step in that direction: intensely personal, largely wordless and driven by the need to work through difficult emotions rather than narrative. Do you see this EP as the culmination of a journey that began with those recent releases, or did it emerge from a fundamentally different place? I don’t think of it as a culmination so much as another point of arrival. Each project tends to emerge from whatever questions I’m living with at the time. All Our Knives… was very outward-facing. It was about community, about bringing different voices into conversation around ideas of resilience and collective memory. Bloom and the instrumental work that followed became quieter spaces where I could sit with loss, change and the slower work of transformation. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE came from an even more internal place. I wasn’t trying to tell a story or resolve anything. I was more interested in documenting a state of being and exorcising some pent-up feelings that were essentially causing me harm. The music became a way of staying present with difficult emotions rather than translating them into language. In that sense it feels connected to the recent releases, but I wasn’t consciously trying to complete a trilogy or close a chapter. It simply became the form those experiences needed. One of the recurring threads across recent works—from The Loops (Grief) and Looking For Light to the standalone single “Malaise”—is an engagement with emotional turbulence that is neither entirely despairing nor entirely hopeful. The title track of A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE speaks of moving through fire rather than escaping it. Has your understanding of grief, burnout and recovery changed over the course of these releases, and do you think this EP arrives at a different emotional destination than those earlier works? I think grief has become less about something to overcome and more about something you learn to live alongside. Earlier work probably carried a stronger desire to find resolution or to move towards the light. I don’t think I see it that way anymore. Recovery isn’t linear, and neither is burnout. There are moments of joy inside exhaustion and moments of uncertainty inside healing. The image of moving through fire rather than escaping it felt important because some experiences can’t be bypassed. They change you. The music on this EP isn’t trying to extinguish the fire; it’s trying to understand what remains after you’ve passed through it. If there’s hope here, it’s a quieter kind. It’s found in endurance, attention and the possibility of continuing to create despite everything. One of the striking aspects of All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was the way you brought together an extraordinary community of Black British voices—Tricky, GAIKA, Ghostpoet, Coby Sey, James Massiah, Space Afrika, Labi Junior and others—creating a record that felt simultaneously personal and collective. More broadly, your recent work has moved freely between songs, spoken-word collaborations, chamber-like compositions, ambient electronics and abstract instrumental forms. By contrast, A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels almost entirely self-contained, built around piano, synthesisers and extended instrumental pieces. After such a collaborative album, did the absence of other voices create a different kind of honesty or vulnerability? Collaboration has always been fundamental to my practice because it allows ideas to exist beyond my own perspective. All Our Knives… couldn’t have existed without those voices. The conversations between people were the point of the record. With this EP I found myself needing the opposite experience. I needed solitude, not because I wanted to withdraw from community, but because I needed to hear what was underneath all the noise. Working mostly alone meant there was nowhere to hide. Every hesitation, every silence, every decision belonged to me. That can feel vulnerable, but it can also be very freeing because you’re no longer trying to explain yourself through words or through other people’s interpretations. I also needed space to cry and I find that’s a hard thing for me to do in front of people, I let go of my masks the most in solitude. So it became a conversation with the instruments themselves. The piano, synthesizers and space all became collaborators in a different sense. You’ve described this EP as a collection of “raging exhalations, quiet revelations, subtle smirks of humility, laments and meditations.” Unlike many of your previous releases, there are no guest vocalists, no lyrics and no obvious narrative anchors. Did working without words feel liberating or exposing? And at this stage in your career, do you feel instrumental music has become just as capable as song of carrying the political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always been central to your work? Working without words was both liberating and exposing. Lyrics can sometimes direct people towards a particular meaning, whereas instrumental music leaves much more room for the listener’s own experience. That openness was something I wanted to embrace. I’ve become increasingly interested in what music communicates before language enters. Breath, texture, resonance, silence… these things carry meaning too. They can hold emotion in ways that words sometimes can’t. I don’t really separate instrumental music from song anymore. They’re just different ways of asking the same questions. The political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always interested me don’t disappear when language disappears. They become embodied differently. Sometimes a sustained note or a shift in harmony can express something that would become smaller if I tried to explain it. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: 这张EP由四首器乐作品组成，核心乐器为钢琴与合成器，辅以大量空间留白。专辑放弃了语言叙事，转向以和声共鸣、力度变化与静默来传达尚未成形为词语的情感——悲伤、疲惫与恢复始终悬而未决。各曲之间保持一致的调性逻辑，但并非传统组曲结构；情绪被刻意克制，不追求戏剧性高潮或炫技段落，而是以亲密感与微小的和声转变推动内在挖掘。整体呈现出内向、冥想式的状态记录，延续了作者从外向社群书写向内化器乐探索的轨迹，在克制中完成情感的转化与释放。

items.album: The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro
items.excerpt: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arr
items.body: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arranged for soprano and double bass. Beyond the hall stood the wooded seclusion of southern Vermont; within it, soprano Lucy Fitz Gibbon and bassist William Langlie Miletich moved between Sprechstimme, art song, extended technique, and charged silence. Seclusion mattered because Kurtág’s music alters the proportions of attention. The claim embedded in the program’s title was stranger than its apparent simplicity suggested. The phrase “world of” ordinarily announces breadth, an oeuvre surveyed from above. Kurtág offers no such cartographic comfort. His world emerges through radical compression, forming under pressure between a sound and its possible disappearance. A few pitches can contain the moral weight of a dramatic scene. A pause can bend duration until time folds inward, secreting another time inside itself. His miniatures remain small only to the clock. To enter them is to accept unfamiliar laws under which fragments carry the mass of vanished wholes and inhalation behaves as active matter. The surrounding forest supplied an uncannily precise grammar for this experience. Every trunk concealed years in concentric script; every root continued a sentence underground. Kurtág’s art operates within a related economy of the imperceptible. A phrase ends, yet its pressure travels elsewhere. Music becomes the audible extremity of processes occurring beneath language. The sequence approached that hidden economy gently through Lembit Beecher’s With Grandchildren, drawn from his 2014 cycle Looking at Spring: Meditations on Aging. The larger work grew from interviews librettist Liza Balkan conducted with senior citizens in Toronto and central Vermont, making its appearance in Marlboro feel almost homeward. Their voices had passed into text and music before returning to the region transformed, bearing traces of their speakers without claiming to preserve them intact. Harmonics in the bass courted a rocking motion whose comfort never became secure, while Fitz Gibbon searched amid the delicate failures of memory. The soul became an unfinished sentence poised beneath scissors, family albums reduced to particles of touch and chronology. Bone creaked as marrow acquired a secret literacy, becoming a divining instrument for the inaccessible past. Beecher respected recollection as an unstable act in which forgetting shapes experience as decisively as retention. Miletich’s pale overtones gave the bass an elderly nervous system of its own. The final word escaped capture, suspending language where recognition touches disappearance. John Cage’s The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs opened another passage into that borderland. Composed in 1942, its text comes from a nocturnal passage concerning Isobel in Finnegans Wake, a book of sleeping consciousness and linguistic mutation. Cage answered that abundance with severe economy. The voice circles within three pitches, while the original accompaniment is played on a closed piano tapped by the player. In Marlboro, those impulses migrated to the double bass, where Miletich turned his instrument of choice into a hollow nocturnal chamber. What had once been struck wood surrounding dormant strings now came from an assemblage held against the player’s body, each impact becoming a coded knock from somewhere inside itself. Fitz Gibbon sustained Cage’s narrow compass with remarkable intensity. Repetition wandered in place, circling a road inferred from every failed attempt to leave it. James Joyce’s words acquired the phosphorescence of objects glimpsed among trees. Isobel became a consciousness translated into the landscape, as identity passed into leaf matter and the boundary between a sleeping mind and the forest dreaming it lost authority. Amy Beth Kirsten’s yes I said yes I will Yes followed as a second excavation of Joyce, drawing on Molly Bloom’s concluding monologue in Ulysses. Written in 2012 for soprano and contrabass, with the bassist also vocalizing, it entered an illuminating dialogue with Cage. Both composers extract a concentrated vocal world from Joyce’s literary machinery. Whereas Cage cools language toward incantation, Kirsten restores its heat while fracturing the body that generates it. Isobel’s suspension yields to Molly’s consciousness in bed, where memory moves through eros and resistance before reaching the irrevocable “Yes.” Fitz Gibbon and Miletich rendered that sensuality as a condition divided against itself. Pizzicato entered beside Miletich’s droning hum, while glissandi bent the music from stable coordinates. Fitz Gibbon inhabited desire while observing its mechanisms from afar, consciousness hovering above its own flesh. The deeply inflected conclusion unfolded as slow-motion blues, each pitch bearing the drag of pleasure becoming memory before experience could have its say. These works prepared the ear for Kurtág’s Einige Sätze aus den Sudelbüchern Georg Christoph Lichtenbergs, Op. 37a, begun in 1996 and expanded for soprano and double bass in 1999. The cycle arose from his encounter with the private notebooks of Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, the 18th-century physicist whose intellect moved between experiment and satire. Never intended for publication, these “waste books” gathered observations whose brevity sharpened their reach. Lichtenberg’s scrutiny ranges across provincialism and religion, colonialism and literary history. Each joke becomes a trapdoor opening onto centuries of vanity. Kurtág began setting the aphorisms while ill, initially for solo soprano. Singer Maria Husmann encouraged the addition of double bass after experimenting with improvised accompaniment, a genesis audible in the finished cycle. Voice and instrument discover one another without settling into fixed roles. The bass accompanies before interrupting, then places a dark question mark beneath Lichtenberg’s wit. Fitz Gibbon and Miletich inhabited these relations with theatrical aptitude. The opening “Die Kartoffeln” (“The Potatoes”) was oddly beautiful in its evocation of slumbering tubers and their potential afterlife. “Kirchtürme” (“Church Spires”) rose through lovely pizzicato, its aspiration destabilized by the plucking that produced it. “Koan” became a fervent prayer edging toward cognitive seizure. Kurtág exposed the nervous system inside each of these, revealing the involuntary twitch beneath polished intelligence. That method reached sardonic clarity in “…und eine neue Welt…” (“…and a New World…”), where Fitz Gibbon sang through her teeth: “The American who discovered Columbus made a nasty discovery.” The reversal compresses colonial history into a grammatical ambush, exposing discovery as a story power tells about intrusion. Here, as elsewhere in the cycle, language appeared to turn against the assumptions concealed within its own syntax. Beecher’s stop-motion films, still a work in progress and therefore accompanying only selected aphorisms, extended this instability into a visual register. His reappearance as animator also gave the program a satisfying circular architecture. Having entered through his own music in With Grandchildren, he returned within Kurtág’s, translating acts of listening into movement and matter. Objects advanced through minute discontinuities, their apparent motion created by absences between frames. The art form therefore proved uncannily suited to Kurtág, whose music repeatedly asks the listener to construct continuity across charged gaps. Both forms make disappearance part of their syntax. The most persuasive union of image and sound came in “Ein Liebhaber der klassischen Philologie” (“A Classical Philology Aficionado”), concerning a man so enamored of Homer that he reads the German angenommen as “Agamemnon.” Books towered behind drifting clouds while statues looked on as thought acquiring mineral flesh. Beecher let the visual analog unfold slowly, giving the words time to expose the strange pathology hidden inside cultivated learning. Erudition became a benign haunting, a possession so complete that antiquity rewrote the present from within. The sequence clarified what the animations contributed to the cycle as a whole: they gave Kurtág’s microscopic dramas another surface upon which to misremember and mutate. The closing “Ein merkwürdiger Gedanke” (“A Strange Thought”) brought Kurtág’s humor to its darkest edge. Miletich and Fitz Gibbon allowed laughter to reveal its ancient kinship with fear. By then, one work had entered another through hidden roots. Cage’s knocks survived inside Kirsten’s tapping, while Beecher’s elderly voices continued inside Lichtenberg’s posthumous sentences. And through it all, Joyce’s sleeping forest returned in the Vermont woods surrounding the hall. The program cohered through subterranean recurrence, with each composition sending material below the surface for another to absorb. Marlboro’s seclusion ultimately changed the concert. Isolation became an acoustic form of relation, concentrating distant minds into one chamber. Beneath our feet, roots continued their exchanges without witnesses, each message altered by the body carrying it. The afternoon suggested that memory follows the same obscure traffic. We imagine ourselves as its custodians, although the reverse may lie closer to the truth. Memory could be the larger organism, ancient and unfinished, using each of us as a temporary organ through which to migrate. For one hour in Ragle Hall, voices became gills in that organism. The post The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 988Tangerine Dream is a progressive electronic rock band that was founded in Berlin, Germany in 1967 by Edgar Froese, Klaus Schulze and Conrad Schnitzler. The band was among the earlier explorers of a new musical universe opened by electronic instruments. Tangerine Dream's music was born as a psychedelic journey in the heavens, and, aided by the new electronic keyboards, the band transformed into a contemplative survey of the universe. By borrowing from the impressionistic painting, (notably of Salvador Dali), the ecclesiastic music, the minimalist avant-garde, and the Eastern transcendental philosophy, Tangerine Dream invented "kosmische music", one of the most influential musical genres.Tangerine Dream released their debut studio work "Electronic Meditation" in 1970 with Froese, Schulze and Schnitzler. Still, "Electronic Meditation" isn't properly an electronic album. It consists mainly of experimental noises performed with classic rock instruments. So, it's more a rock album made with rock instruments. Actually it's a krautrock album, the musical style invented by the German musicians in the late of the 60's and early of the 70's. It was only on their second album "Alpha Centauri" that the synthesizers came into play. After the release of "Electronic Meditation", each member went his own separate way. The only member that remained in Tangerine Dream was Froese. With Froese, Christopher Franke and Steve Schroyder on the line up, the band released their second work "Alpha Centauri"."Alpha Centauri" is the second album of Tangerine Dream, released in 1971. The line up is Edgar Froese (voice, guitar, bass, organ, Fx and Mellotron), Steve Schroyder (voice, Hammond & Farfisa organs, electronics and percussion) and Christopher Franke (flute, piano, harp, zither, VCS 3 synthesizer, drums and percussion). "Alpha Centauri" also had the participation of Udo Dennenberg (voice and flute), Roland Paulick (VCS 3 synthesizer) and Peter Baumann (organ).As I mentioned above, "Alpha Centauri" is the first really electronic progressive rock album released by the band and where we can see for the first time the use of synthesizers by Tangerine Dream. The line up on the album consisted of a guitarist, a percussionist, a flutist and three keyboardists recording the three improvised jams of "Alpha Centauri" that defined the genre. Here, we can also see the presence, for the first time, of what is considered the best line up of the band, Froese, Franke and Baumann, despite the latter only appearing as guest. As happened with their debut work, "Alpha Centauri" became the only album with this official line up, Froese, Franke and Schroyder. And it became also tremendously closer to what Tangerine Dream would be all about than what their debut had been. Sure, it still sounded rather primitive and low-budget, but Tangerine Dream had now clearly discovered that spacey, atmospheric and dreamy experimental electronic music was the way to go for them. It would be completely proven with their next album "Zeit"."Alpha Centauri" has three tracks. "Sunrise In The Third System" contains some slow spacey sounds and effects. It's a stealthy and hypnotic piece, with a dense organ and a ghostly flute. It has a clear nod to Pink Floyd thanks to the sound of the organ. It forms a perfect introduction to the main cosmic journey, a kind of decompression chamber that helps the listener get acclimated to the alien landscape of Tangerine Dream's musical world. "Fly And Collision Of Comas Sola" slowly builds a heroic theme that eventually crashes into chaos. The track starts with a synthesizer and an organ in the background. The organ makes its appearance to establish the mattress on which flutes and synths build enveloping and disturbing sounds. As the song progresses, the drums appear closing with an abrupt ending. It allows us to envision great things in the future band's history. The title track is the centre piece of the album. It's an interesting improvisation based around spacey electronic sounds, organs and Froese's guitar. At the end goes into a poem spoken in German and climaxes into one of the few cases of human vocal-harmonies on a band's album. The flute makes a fine atmospheric contrast. It's an incredible spacey and timeless experience. You got the impression of leaving this world. It paves way for everything on their next album "Zeit" to all their famous lengthy epics like the title track on "Phaedra".Conclusion: As I mentioned above, "Alpha Centauri" is considered as the first electronic space album. It marks the transition from the krautrock to the electronic bubbling sound of their albums "Zeit" and "Atem" in their Pink phase. If "Electronic Meditation" had seemed better suited to a horror film, "Alpha Centauri" is firmly in the science fiction camp. The structure of the album would prove to be very representative for the several albums to come from the band, with one side long title track and a couple of "shorter" tracks on the other side. So, despite some technical shortcomings, "Alpha Centauri" was an important release in the musical evolution of Tangerine Dream. The mysterious cover painting and art design, by Edgar Froese and his wife at the time, Monique Froese, contribute directly to the album's character. As products of the psych era, "Alpha Centauri", "Zeit" and "Atem", are fine nuggets, even if the best was yet to come.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items._cn_summary: 本文是ProgArchives网站上关于Tangerine Dream 1971年专辑《Alpha Centauri》的乐评。乐评首先追溯了乐队从1967年柏林成立的历史脉络，介绍了前身专辑《Electronic Meditation》的实验噪声特征，随后聚焦于本张专辑作为乐队真正迈入电子合成器领域的转折点。文中详细列出了阵容配置——Froese、Schroyder与Franke为核心成员，辅以Dennenberg、Paulick和Baumann等客座乐手，并指出三位键盘演奏者与吉他、打击乐、长笛形成的三段即兴jam结构。乐评强调该专辑虽然制作仍显原始和低成本，但已清晰确立了Tangerine Dream标志性的太空感、氛围化与梦幻化的电子实验音乐方向，被视为krautrock与kosmische musik流派的关键奠基作品之一。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many factors at play with this soundtrack. First of all, it is worth noting that soundtracks often inspire great electronic music albums, given the genre's inherently cinematic and atmospheric nature, as seen with Klaus Schulze's Body Love. Edgar Froese, his bandmate in Tangerine Dream, turned the score for Wolf Gremm's film into his own sixth solo album. The movie also marked the final screen appearance of the German director Rainer Werner Fassbinder as an actor. Based on the novel Murder on the 31st Floor by Per Wahl��, the story is set in a future Germany where a private corporation holds power and all societal problems appear to have been solved, until a group calling itself "Kamikaze" issues a bomb threat. Detective Jansen (Fassbinder), clad in his signature leopard-print suit, then uncovers unexpected and deeply sinister connections and mysteries. The track "Videophonic" immediately immerses the listener in a sci-fi atmosphere; the music transcends standard synthesizer-based electronics, evoking the mysterious, perilous vibe of Krautrock."Vitamin C" is almost danceable, yet driven by a magnetic, funky groove; beneath the main rhythm lies a synthesizer wash that adds a progressive sheen, allowing the track to build, shift, evolve, and unfold organically. "Krismopompas" reminded me of Air, even though this album predates them, featuring dissonant notes; while knowing the film's plot helps, the track stands perfectly well on its own thanks to its strong melodic content. "Police Disco" shows traces of Vangelis but possesses an restless quality that lends it extreme dynamism; subtle classical influences lurk in the background, and there are echoes of Pink Floyd, specifically the Echoes era, giving the album an experimental edge that makes it compelling.With its electronic percussion, Police Therapy Center feels more rooted in the 80s; yet, there are underlying keyboard layers, like out-of-tune violins, providing subtle accompaniment, while the style shifts instantly to a highly martial funeral march on "Blue Panther." "Unexpected Death" is almost psychedelic, a realm where electronics also lend themselves well, acting as a malleable, mutating substance.Flying Kamikaze is ambient music with a spacey, ethereal vibe, reminiscent of Popol Vuh's work on Fitzcarraldo. Yet it is dark and mysterious, reflecting both the natural world and the ominous Berlin of this dark utopia. "Tower Block" conveys that feverish, concrete-laden urban atmosphere translated into music, while the closing track "The 31st Floor", which alludes to the original novel, broadens the horizon; blending electronica with the futuristic Krautrock style of Can's "Spoon" (from Ege Bamyasi) and straddling the line between film noir and dystopian sci-fi, Kamikaze 1989 showcased many of Froese's great strengths as a composer dedicated to illustrating mental imagery while maintaining his artistic independence.

items._cn_summary: 这是Edgar Froese为1982年德国科幻电影《Kamikaze 1989》创作的原声专辑，也是Tangerine Dream成员的个人第六张专辑。乐评指出，影片设定在未来德国，私人企业掌控社会，侦探Fassbinder身着标志性豹纹西装追查炸弹威胁，故事具有反乌托邦色彩。音乐层面，开篇的Videophonic营造出强烈的科幻氛围，超越了常规合成器电子乐的范畴，带有Krautrock的神秘感；Vitamin C以放克律动驱动，合成器音色层叠推进；Krismopollas旋律性强且带有不和谐音；Police Disco展现Vangelis式光泽与Pink Floyd式的实验边缘；Flying Kamikaze则走向ambient领域，与Popol Vuh的氛围遥相呼应；终曲The 31st Floor融合Krautrock与电子，呈现黑色电影与反乌托邦科幻交织的气质。整张专辑展现了Froese作为作曲家将视觉意象转化为声音的能力，同时保持了独立艺术个性。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑被描述为需要大量聆听才能接受的'获得性品味'作品，评论者经历了从厌恶到容忍再到认可的过程，经过约三十次聆听后将其视为前卫摇滚领域的杰作。专辑以Captain Beefheart标志性的怪诞人声为核心，融合了乐队成员高超而自由的器乐演奏，整体呈现出难以用语言准确描述的实验性美学。评论者特别提到了其中一首名为Sweet Sweet Bulbs的曲目，认为是整张专辑中最具代表性的作品。评论者同时表达了对Beefheart其他作品的探索兴趣，并对其演唱中的幽默人声处理印象深刻。整体而言，这是一张充满个性与冒险精神的实验专辑，适合愿意投入时间反复聆听的听众。

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Wish You Were Here is one of those albums that does not need to be excessively complex to feel progressive. Released in 1975, it combines progressive rock, psychedelic rock, art rock and space rock into an incredibly cohesive and atmospheric experience. I would not consider it one of Pink Floyd's most overtly progressive albums, but its careful compositions, long instrumental developments, experimental production and thematic coherence make it a very strong progressive rock work.The atmosphere is probably the album's greatest strength. It is contemplative, melancholic, emotional and, at times, almost intellectual in the way its themes are presented. The production has aged remarkably well, with every instrument occupying its own space in the mix. The synthesizers and keyboards of Richard Wright are particularly impressive, adding an essential dimension to the album's sound.The centerpiece is undoubtedly "Shine On You Crazy Diamond", which I consider a masterpiece in its own right. I prefer to experience its different sections as one complete work rather than treating them as separate pieces. The song contains excellent instrumental development, especially in the guitars, drums and synthesizers. David Gilmour's guitar work is outstanding, combining technical ability with an enormous amount of emotional expression. Wright's keyboards are equally important, creating much of the psychedelic and spacious atmosphere that defines the piece.The emotional weight of "Shine On You Crazy Diamond" is also increased by its connection to Syd Barrett, whose work with Pink Floyd I greatly admire. Knowing that the song was written as a tribute to him gives the piece an additional emotional dimension. The feeling of loss and nostalgia is deeply present without overwhelming the music itself."Welcome to the Machine" is another major highlight. Its synthesizer work is simply magnificent, and the electronic textures create an almost mechanical atmosphere that perfectly complements the song's subject matter. The composition is less progressive in a traditional structural sense, but its sound design and atmosphere are remarkably creative. I would give the synthesizers an almost absurd 10/10 ? or, jokingly, 1,000,000/10. This is one of the clearest examples of how Pink Floyd could use studio production itself as part of the composition.The lyrics also contribute considerably to the album's thematic unity. Alongside the tribute to Syd Barrett, the record deals with the music industry and the way it can become destructive and dehumanizing. "Welcome to the Machine" and "Have a Cigar" are particularly effective in this regard. Even though these themes were written in the 1970s, they remain strikingly relevant today."Have a Cigar" is another very enjoyable track. Roy Harper's vocals work surprisingly well and have some similarities to Roger Waters' voice. The song is more accessible than some of the album's other material, but it still fits naturally into the overall concept.The title track, "Wish You Were Here", is probably the most commercially accessible song on the album. I personally rate it slightly below the other tracks, at 7/10, but it still serves an important role in the album as a whole. Its lyrics and emotional character provide another perspective on the themes of absence, loss and alienation.One of the things I appreciate most about Wish You Were Here is how naturally the tracks connect to each other. The album can almost feel like one long composition, rather than simply a collection of individual songs. The transitions, recurring atmosphere and production choices create an unusually strong sense of unity.From a progressive perspective, I would describe the album as moderately progressive. It is not constantly concerned with complex time signatures, virtuosity or extremely elaborate structures. Instead, its progressive qualities come from the development of ideas, extended instrumental passages, experimentation with sound, thematic coherence and the willingness to let atmosphere become a fundamental part of the composition.The instrumentation is excellent throughout. Gilmour's guitars are a major highlight, Wright's keyboards and synthesizers are perhaps the most distinctive element of the album for me, Nick Mason's drumming contributes effectively to the long developments, and the saxophone adds another color to the sound. The engineering and production are also outstanding, particularly in the way the instruments and effects are separated and integrated into the overall soundscape.The album's strongest qualities are "Shine On You Crazy Diamond," Richard Wright's synthesizers and keyboards, and David Gilmour's guitars and vocals. I honestly don't have any significant weaknesses to point out. Even though "Wish You Were Here" itself is the most commercial track and the one I personally rate lowest, it is still an important part of the complete experience.Overall, Wish You Were Here is an album in which you can become completely absorbed in the atmosphere of the music. It is contemplative, melancholic, psychedelic and emotionally powerful, while remaining carefully composed and remarkably cohesive.Alongside Meddle and Atom Heart Mother, it is among my favorite Pink Floyd albums.Essential for anyone interested in atmospheric and psychedelic progressive rock.
items._genre: progressive rock / psychedelic rock / art rock / space rock
items._cn_summary: 这张1975年的专辑将前卫摇滚、迷幻摇滚、艺术摇滚与太空摇滚融为一体，营造出高度统一的氛围体验。评论者认为它并非Pink Floyd最具明显前卫性的作品，但凭借精心编排的作曲、长篇器乐发展、实验性制作以及主题连贯性，成为一部扎实的前卫摇滚作品。氛围是专辑最大的优势——沉思、忧郁、情感丰富，制作精良使每件乐器在混音中各占其位，Wright的合成器与键盘尤为突出。核心曲目《Shine On You Crazy Diamond》被视为杰作，Gilmour的吉他与Wright的键盘共同构建出迷幻而宽广的空间感，同时融入了对Syd Barrett的致敬情感。《Welcome to the Machine》展示了将录音棚制作本身作为作曲手段的创意，合成器音色设计极具机械感。《Have a Cigar》则更易接近，Roy Harper的演唱恰到好处。歌词层面，专辑同时探讨了音乐工业的异化主题，在当下仍具现实意义。

items.body: The Sound Veil Society‘s debut album “Things We Kept” is built around an unusual kind of intensity. The record rarely reaches for aggression or dramatic excess; instead, emotional weight accumulates through restraint, space, repetition and the careful relationship between voice, electronics and silence. That became even clearer to me after seeing the duo at E-Only before spending more time with the album. Live, the songs seemed capable of becoming physically larger without sacrificing the intimacy they carry on record. The Swedish-Norwegian project brings together Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson, two musicians with extensive histories in Nordic electronic music, but “Things We Kept” does not sound like an exercise in accumulated experience or genre expertise. The more interesting question is what happens when experience becomes instinct: when musicians know enough to stop demonstrating what they know and instead concentrate on what a song actually needs. Released on 11 September 2026 through Progress Productions, “Things We Kept” is the duo’s first full-length album. Its title becomes more revealing as the record unfolds. What we keep is not necessarily what we consciously choose to preserve. Memory, grief, unfinished conversations, attachments and previous versions of ourselves remain present long after circumstances have changed. That tension between movement and emotional permanence runs quietly through an album whose apparent delicacy repeatedly turns out to carry considerable force. The Sound Veil Society interview Karo: I saw you at E-Only before hearing “Things We Kept”, and what struck me was that the performance generated enormous emotional pressure without relying on aggression or theatrical excess. Is restraint something you consciously build into The Sound Veil Society, or is it simply where the two of you naturally meet? The Sound Veil Society: It’s the natural way for us to express ourselves, and TSVS is the outlet where we can give these feelings and emotions free space in our performance, both on record and live. Karo: “Things We Kept” is a debut album made by musicians who are anything but beginners. Does starting a new project after years of experience give you greater freedom, or does experience make it harder to surprise yourselves because you already know too well what works? The Sound Veil Society: Good question! In a way, it gives us more freedom, as we use our experience together with what we have learned over the years to create something new. But it might just be the circle of life, as we evolve through different phases in our lives, with new experiences and so on. And it would be boring to repeat ourselves, so to trigger creativity and motivation, we just do what we like and hopefully someone else likes it as well. Karo: The album feels remarkably coherent across music, lyrics, photography, videos and the physical booklet. Did you think of “Things We Kept” as a complete world from the beginning, or did that visual and emotional language gradually reveal itself while the music was taking shape? The Sound Veil Society: We did have an idea from the beginning to be very visual in what we do as TSVS. The album itself is a result of our journey in making it. After a year or so of making a lot of demos, we decided where we wanted to take our sound, and after that everything just fell into place. “Things We Kept” became a complete world through the process and, indeed, there is a thought behind the booklet, videos and music completing each other. Karo: There is something almost paradoxical about this record: it sounds delicate, but never weak. I kept thinking of tempered glass: transparent, apparently fragile, yet internally capable of carrying enormous force. Where does that balance between vulnerability and strength come from in your writing? The Sound Veil Society: Really like your reflection of the record! It reflects quite well who we are as people, in a way, as both of us are emotional beings, with our share of struggles both in the past and present. But that can also be used as a strength, because you need a certain amount of strength to deal with the challenges in life. So for us it is a very natural process and nothing we “try” to do. It just happens that way. Karo: The lyrics repeatedly return to movement: leaving, running, waiting, returning, searching for air. Yet emotionally, many of the characters seem unable to escape what they carry with them. Were you consciously interested in the difference between physically moving on and actually changing? The Sound Veil Society: Not really. It is just our way of describing thoughts and feelings that are close to us, or stories and reflections that have inspired us over the years. Karo: The title “Things We Kept” becomes more interesting the longer one spends with the record, because what people keep is often not something they would consciously choose: grief, unfinished conversations, versions of other people, even destructive attachments. What does “keeping” mean to you in the context of this album? The Sound Veil Society: We think that everything we experience, be it good or bad, stays with us to some degree, even when we have almost forgotten about it, because it shapes us into who we are right now. Without all the experiences we go through in life, we would not be the same people we are today. Karo: Erlend’s voice is very exposed in these songs, but the arrangements rarely try to underline every emotion he expresses. How do you decide when the music should support the voice and when it should deliberately leave it almost alone? The Sound Veil Society: It’s all about the feeling, really, and nothing we think too much about when we make music. To express ourselves the way we want, it just tends to become like that. Karo: One thing I noticed both at E-Only and on the album is how important space is. The songs are not afraid of air, pauses or sounds that are allowed to remain isolated. In electronic music, where it is technically very easy to keep adding layers, is knowing what to remove as important to you as knowing what to write? The Sound Veil Society: In a way it is, but the most important thing for us is to write a good song and express the feeling we want to express with it. We do use quite a lot of layers, but they are often subtle and just there to emphasise the sound. Since we have some years behind us making music, we have learned that sometimes less is more. Karo: The visual material often uses roads, water, landscapes, silhouettes and people partly disappearing from view. They feel less like illustrations of individual songs than fragments of memory. How closely do you work on the relationship between image and sound, and what can an image express that you deliberately leave unresolved in the lyrics? The Sound Veil Society: It depends on the idea of the song we are working on, but we often get visual ideas while making music. An image or a video clip itself is a great way to describe emotions, and combining sound and visuals simply makes a story more complete. Karo: Your musical backgrounds give you access to an established electronic vocabulary, yet “Things We Kept” does not sound interested in demonstrating genre knowledge. Was there anything from your previous projects that you consciously had to unlearn in order for The Sound Veil Society to develop its own identity? The Sound Veil Society: Not much, really. The only thing we have been trying to do is shorten parts, as it is easy to keep things simply because they sound good, but in the end they often just make a track less interesting. Other than that, everything else just fell into place during the making of it. Karo: At E-Only I had the impression that some of these songs actually became larger through performance without losing their intimacy. Has playing the material in front of people changed your understanding of the album, perhaps shown you emotional qualities in certain songs that were less obvious in the studio? The Sound Veil Society: It can happen, but we often already have an idea of how a song will work live when we make it. So most of our work is made just as much for the live stage as it is for a record, actually. Of course, before the first live show, we didn’t know how our vision would translate to the audience, but after these shows we really feel that we get a special connection with the audience. Karo: “Things We Kept” establishes a very precise emotional and visual identity for a first album. Looking ahead, does that identity now feel like a foundation you want to deepen, or something you already feel tempted to disturb? What are you curious to discover about The Sound Veil Society next? The Sound Veil Society: In a way, it is a foundation to build upon and is, in many ways, the core of our concept. But we do want to evolve and make something new along the way, so we don’t yet know what it will become. But that is also part of the fun: exploring new sides of a concept. We will always aim to be as honest and raw in our expression. About The Sound Veil Society The Sound Veil Society is a Swedish-Norwegian electronic duo formed in 2024 by Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson. Eilertsen is associated with Essence Of Mind and Lights A.M. and joined Xenturion Prime in 2024; Mattsson co-founded Code 64, later established Xenturion Prime and has also been involved with Essence Of Mind. The project debuted with “The River” on 24 April 2025, followed by “OK” on 22 August 2025 and “Hunger for Light” in March 2026. Their debut album, “Things We Kept”, was released by Progress Productions on 11 September 2026. The standard edition contains eleven tracks, including “Voices” featuring KÅRP; the CD adds three bonus versions, while the album was also issued on black-and-white splatter vinyl and as a limited MiniDisc edition. The duo performed at Nocturnal Culture Night and E-Only Festival; a live video for “Nothing to Say” was recorded at E-Only in Leipzig in March 2026. The Sound Veil Society are already confirmed for Eastside Festival in Halle (Saale), Germany, on 2-3 July 2027.
items._cn_summary: The Sound Veil Society首张全长专辑由挪威与瑞典两位资深电子音乐人Erlend Eilertsen与Hans-Olof Mattsson合作完成，于Progress Productions发行。整张作品回避侵略性与戏剧化铺陈，转而通过节制、留白、重复与声学沉默积累情感重量，人声、电子音效与静默之间形成精微张力。标题"Things We Kept"暗示记忆、悲伤、未竟对话与旧日自我并非主动留存之物，而是持续在场，专辑即围绕这种流动与情感恒久性之间的张力展开。乐评人指出两位音乐人虽经验丰富，作品却不流于炫技，而是让经验化为本能，专注歌曲真正所需。现场演出将录音室内的亲密感扩展为更具身体性的体验。整体而言，这是一张以极简手法承载巨大情感压力的北欧独立电子作品。

items.body: There’s always a moment when an artist with a reputation for electronic music severity discovers the cheap thrill of a perfect pop song, and Chances finds Kontravoid standing over the evidence with a butcher’s knife in his hand, dripping blood-red from your severed expectations. Behind that mask, it’s difficult to tell whether Cameron Findlay looks pleased with himself, but the hook suggests he’s been planning this for some time. Findlay has spent years making electronic music built from locked doors, hard angles, and basslines with the social instincts of a nightclub bouncer. Chances, the latest preview from Sound of the Void, due October 2 through Artoffact Records, loosens that grip without turning soft. There’s a trace of Cabaret Voltaire’s “Why Kill Time” in its marriage of electronic unease and pop temptation, the sense that a tune can slip something deeply questionable past you simply by making your hips complicit. The bassline supplies the charm, the synthesizers raise suspicions, and by the time the hook takes hold, you’re already eating a stranger’s piece of candy in the back of a white van. The surprise is not that Kontravoid can write pop. The surprise is how naturally this thing fits this masked marvel. The song opens with clipped, almost cryptic lines pushed through a harsh vocal treatment, Findlay’s voice sounding less sung than transmitted from some badly damaged communications device. Around him, warped synthesizers bend and smear, but the track never loses its discipline. The bass is lush and melodic, the electro beat keeps the body moving, and the arrangement has enough open space to let the hooks land cleanly. Then the verse seems to come apart at the seams. His voice gives way to a wash of effects and a series of shouts, as if the song has briefly forgotten the difference between a chorus and an alert from the Emergency Broadcast System. This is pop music with the wiring exposed. It has the sleek economy of synthpop, but Findlay refuses to sand down the abrasion that makes Kontravoid recognizable. The sinister pads and forceful rhythms still carry the weight of coldwave and EBM, only now they are being used in service of something broader, catchier, and frankly more dangerous because it might get stuck in your head before you realize how severe it is. That expansion also makes sense for a project that has never been as one-dimensional as the mask suggests. From Undone through Too Deep and Faceless, Findlay has always buried melody inside the machinery; Chances simply drags it forward and lets the damn thing breathe. Listen to “Chances” below and pre-order Sound of the Void, due out October 2 via Artoffact Records, here. Sound of the Void will be available digitally, on CD, and on clear vinyl. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Following Detachment in 2024, Findlay’s second full-length for Artoffact gives melody more room to move through the Kontravoid universe, and Chances makes a persuasive case for taking the chance of leaving your doors unlocked. There’s a blade concealed beneath the song’s immaculate pop tailoring, however, and anyone attempting to call the genre police will find the phone line has been cut. Kontravoid is currently on tour in North America, co-headlining with Australian electronic artist Buzz Kull. The run concludes October 24 at the SUBSTANCE festival in Los Angeles. The October 2 album release falls on the tour’s Kansas City stop. Spike Hellis and Normal Bias will join the bill in Spokane, Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, and Sacramento. Tickets and further information are available through Kontravoid’s official website. Tour Dates: September 22 — Foufounes Électriques — Montreal, QC September 24 — Cafeteria — Toronto, ON September 25 — Funhouse at Mr. Smalls — Pittsburgh, PA September 26 — Anodyne Coffee Roasting Co. — Milwaukee, WI September 28 — Icehouse — Minneapolis, MN October 1 — The 808 — Indianapolis, IN October 2 — Encore at Uptown Theater — Kansas City, MO October 3 — HQ — Denver, CO October 4 — Metro Music Hall — Salt Lake City, UT October 6 — Big Dipper — Spokane, WA* October 8 — Biltmore Cabaret — Vancouver, BC* October 9 — El Corazon — Seattle, WA* October 10 — Star Theater — Portland, OR* October 13 — Holland Project — Reno, NV October 15 — Starlet Room — Sacramento, CA* October 16 — Backstage Bar — Las Vegas, NV October 23 — SUBSTANCE at Great American Music Hall — San Francisco, CA October 24 — SUBSTANCE at Belasco Theatre — Los Angeles, CA *With Spike Hellis and Normal Bias. items._cn_summary: Kontravoid 由 Cameron Findlay 主导，延续其冷波与 EBM 血统的同时，在新单曲《Chances》中向合成器流行做出显著倾斜。评论指出，作品并未因此失去锋利感——失真的人声处理、扭曲的合成器音效与警报式爆发仍保留其辨识度，只是被一条丰满旋律化的贝斯线与流畅的电子节拍重新组织。文中将其与 Cabaret Voltaire 的《Why Kill Time》并置，强调不安的电子质感与流行诱惑力之间的张力。该曲作为专辑《Sound of the Void》的预热，展现了项目从冷硬工业向更易吸收但仍具威胁性的方向扩展。整篇文章为独立小厂牌 Artoffact Records 的原创乐评，文字质量扎实，分析聚焦于声音设计与旋律走向的平衡。

items.body: With every breath Thru muck and grime In every trek We write … Greg Bullock has spent enough time around darkwave to know that gloom by itself is cheap, and on 26EP he treats darkness less as decoration than as a blunt instrument for asking ugly questions. Bullock, co-founder of Cyborg Amok, wrote, produced, mixed, performed, and illustrated this four-song set himself at GABWorx Studio B, which gives the record the slightly dangerous feeling of a man locking himself in a room with synthesizers, a bass, an electric mandolin, and several subjects polite company usually keeps under the table. There is nobody here to tell him that mortality, ecological collapse, betrayal, and human endurance might be a bit much for one EP, which is probably why the record has teeth. In Other Words starts with endurance, though Bullock does not turn survival into a greeting-card slogan. Trenches, mud, climbing, breath, effort: the vocabulary suggests a life measured by what it costs to keep moving. The song carries a reflective sweep that places Bullock somewhere between Depeche Mode’s electronic gravity and Roger Waters staring at civilization with his arms folded. There is comfort in the chorus, but the comfort has dirt under its fingernails. Then comes Thirty Pieces, which drags betrayal, punishment, commerce, and crucifixion into the same dry stretch of ground. Bullock uses biblical imagery with the instincts of someone less interested in Sunday-school reverence than in the ugly exchange rate between flesh and money. Silver gets thrown, bodies get displayed, peace gets its monument, and the entire arrangement starts feeling like one of those public ceremonies where everybody solemnly agrees not to mention who paid for the nails. I Ain’t Goin! is the EP’s great crooked grin. Bullock considers death and responds with the cosmic equivalent of hiding behind the couch when the landlord knocks. Angels can drag him away, Saint Peter can check his watch, and eternity can leave another message. Mortality remains right there in the room. Bullock’s electric mandolin and bass give the track a wiry, physical character, and its humour keeps the record from sinking beneath the weight of its own concerns. Blu-Green Beauty turns toward ecological collapse and corporate arithmetic, with burning seas, damaged forests, fossil fuels, solar panels, recycling, and the familiar human talent for closing the curtains while somebody else totals the profits. Bullock’s anger is clearest here, yet he keeps the song anchored to concrete images rather than vague righteousness. The result has the clipped moral unease of classic synth-pop filtered through the suspicious eye of someone reading the financial pages beside an environmental report. Across twenty minutes or so, 26EP keeps returning to responsibility: what we owe the dead, the living, the planet, and ourselves while there is still time to argue about it. Bullock’s hooks keep the philosophy from turning into homework, while his arrangements give each track its own shape and temperature. He has made a compact record about enormous subjects, and the best compliment is that none of them feel safely settled. Listen to 26EP below and order the EP here. items.body: Purest Form Resistance Dais Records Despite its brief fifteen minute runtime, there’s a meal to be made out of LA trio Purest Form’s latest EP, their debut on Dais, both in terms of attitude and presentation, as well as what its selection of very clear influences might portend for the larger post-industrial landscape. Drawing upon familiar markers of 90s electronic aggression, Resistance provides a tight test case for their read on that historical moment. Opener “Animal” functions as a strong calling card for Purest Form, showing both their capacity for a catchy, heavily processed guitar riff as well as Story Beeson’s acidic growl that’s part grindcore, part death metal. Factor in just the right amount of backing programming and an easily chantable chorus and it becomes both cathartic and anthemic in short order. It is, to be glib, exactly the type of thrashing industrial rock glory which KMFDM have been failing to recapture for the past couple of decades. Much of the rest of the EP’s made up of densely programmed two-minute wipeouts jammed up with breaks, more heavily processed guitar now functioning more for colour than riffs, and more spleen and vile being vented. If that sounds on paper fairly akin to digital hardcore, listening to “Break” and “More” will do little to dissuade that presumption. “Beyond Terror” acts as a quick riposte to this frenetic pace, offering post-hardcore chug while the vocals cut through equivocations about the killings of Palestinians – “call it what you like, it’s genocide.” And then there’s the closing cover. Fifteen or twenty years back, an industrial metal act doing a straightforward version of The Prodigy’s “Breathe” would have felt awkwardly retrograde. However, a full three decades on from the original release and overdriven into the red to the point that it’s difficult to distinguish original tracks from sampled ones, Purest Form’s take on “Breathe” feels like the best sort of “oh shit, they’re covering this?” moment at the end of a packed and sweaty basement show. In discussing the appeal of the 90s sources Pures Form borrow from it’s important to not overstate how new they might be to the band; both Beeson and guitarist/programmer Madi Woodward both have lengthy rap sheets with slews of hardcore and metal acts going back a decade or so. But there’s no question that a combination of their backgrounds beyond industrial and the historical space separating Resistance from those acts helps invigorate their dense and furious angle on them. Buy it. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM The post Purest Form, “Resistance” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 洛杉矶三人组 Purest Form 的首张 Dais 厂牌 EP《Resistance》以十五分钟的紧凑篇幅，呈现了对九十年代电子攻击性美学的当代诠释。开场曲《Animal》展示了经过重度处理的吉他 riff 与兼具 grindcore 和死亡金属特质的嘶吼嗓音，搭配洗脑式的副歌，构成一首宣泄性极强的工业摇滚赞歌。其余曲目多为两分钟左右的密集编程爆裂曲，融合了数字硬核的节奏结构与后硬核的沉重切分。《Beyond Terror》放慢节奏，歌词直接指向巴勒斯坦议题。《Breathe》对 The Prodigy 原曲的暴力翻唱将采样与原创音色推至过载极限。乐评指出乐队成员此前活跃于硬核与金属场景，这种跨领域背景为作品注入了新鲜的怒火与密度。

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Jason Rigby: tenor and soprano saxophones; Lisa Parrott: alto, soprano, and baritone saxophones; Russ Johnson: trumpet; Cameron Brown: bass; Tony Jefferson: drums. Bassist and composer Cameron Brown has always felt comfortable in both traditional and avant-garde settings, and was an important element in the rhythm sections behind Archie Shepp, Don Pullen, George Adams, George Russell, Dewey Redman, and Don Cherry. Here, he leads a chordless quintet, paying tribute to Cherry as well as his mentor Dannie Richmond, best known for his extensive work with the one-and-only bassist, composer, and bandleader Charles Mingus. This ensemble started as a quartet featuring saxophonist Jason Rigby, trumpeter Russ Johnson, and drummer Tony Jefferson. Saxophonist Lisa Parrott joins them here for a dense, unfiltered session recorded live in concert in 2011. Raw and dense, it often sounds like a jam. The uptempo “ Sheila, It’s You! ”—written for the late jazz vocalist Sheila Jordan—has the three-horn frontline blowing with hard-bop intensity over the hard-charging swing provided by the rhythm section. They alternate solos before intersecting their searing lines with purpose. Conversely, “ Lullaby For George, Don, and Donnie ” is a 3/4 ballad gently propelled by brushes. “ Baby Suite ” is a through-composed response to Cherry’s “cocktail suite” concept. Brown’s three-minute bass monologue—featuring double-stops and thoughtful melodic development—right after the contrapuntal theme leads into faster bass circularity, with Jefferson free to embellish while the horns float above. A spontaneous avant-garde freedom reminiscent of Mingus’ excursions can be felt in the coda that precedes the theme. “ Cocktail Suite ”, which clocks in at 21 minutes and includes Cherry’s “ Remembrance ” and “ OC/DC ”, Jobim’s “ Portrait in Black and White ”, and Redman’s “ Mushi Mushi ”, features some awkward passages and elongated solos with the horns left to roam freely. Incessant walking lines populate the recording, creating an inescapable sense of anticipation. Brown’s “ Rylie’s Bounce ” blooms with a bass solo at the outset and explosive drumming by Jefferson, who throws in some barbed percussive sounds on Richmond’s “ Soft Seas ”, an amusing calypso dance served with humor and panache. Parrott causes some frisson on baritone, while Rigby explores the opposite end of the spectrum on soprano. This piece is put together much more effectively, with a keen sense of time and a divergence from conventional swing. With the interplay controlled at all times and the recording sounding like a classic, Remembrance sometimes rings a bit meandering, yet never disjointed. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Baby Suite ► 03 - Soft Seas ► 07 - Cocktail Suite
items._cn_summary: 贝斯手兼作曲家Cameron Brown领衔的无和弦五重奏，以2011年现场录音为蓝本，向已故的Don Cherry和Dannie Richmond致敬。整张专辑呈现出粗粝而密集的质感，三支管乐（两支萨克斯与一支小号）在硬波普节奏上激烈交织，独奏段落锋利且充满即兴张力。《Sheila, It's You!》以快速硬波普Swing开场，《Lullaby For George, Don, and Donnie》转为三拍子刷子叙事的抒情段落。《Baby Suite》通过Brown三分钟的低音独白、对位主题与前卫自由展开回应Cherry的'鸡尾酒组曲'概念。《Cocktail Suite》以21分钟篇幅串联多首致敬曲目，管乐自由漫游，偶尔略显冗长。《Rylie's Bounce》与《Soft Seas》以加勒比海卡里普索节奏带来幽默感与即兴爆发力，Jefferson的鼓点极具穿刺力。专辑整体控制得当，经典质感与自由探索并存，尽管偶有散漫之感，但从未断裂。

items.body: While the ambient music subgenre of field recording has already been heavily explored, there is a renewing naivete I find in layering protoconversation and young children’s laughs and chatter onto monoid synth. While children can come out with the most random question of reality at uncertain times, monoid synth drone matching with vocals is something still refreshing and wonderful. The happy/sad neutralising is enigmatic. ‘Field Recording Meets Sound’ is a superb exploration of the will ‘o wisp burn of good ambience in a post-youthquake environment of milleni-mania. The sleepy-eyed and toxic nature of drone impregnates the surface sheen of the quality dorian-led sounds, and the nascent lack of solidified scales lends the music a naively posited professionalism, hence a between-state, a purity of fashion. The opening to the record conjures up a bustling city street, cars passing and humans moving bumper to bumper of the drone’s base-line. There is a cordial overlap between choral music and musique concrete; voice shards blend into a smoothie mush against the very Pausal and Rafael Antoni Irissari esque hum of the record. Meaning to placate emotionally the roundabout encirclement of the somehow managed vocal loops, there is a majesty of tapestry coagulated through forceful re-clustering of the central vocal/synth sound set. A gripping element of the music is its immediate joility and then its spreading of aesthetic colours into a peacock tail kaleidoscope of sometimes languid, occasionally touching and regularly haunting passages. What particularly excites and succeeds about this album is its candour. It sounds innocent. Always of its time; never pretentious. These feelings you get channeled from the drones are contentment based. Recommended! www.krysalisound.com
items._cn_summary: 这是一张在田野录音与合成器氛围之间寻找新可能性的专辑。评论者特别指出，将儿童的对话与笑声叠加在单声道合成器持续音之上的做法，在田野录音已被大量探索的语境下仍显得清新。整张作品呈现出一种快乐与悲伤相互中和的暧昧状态，既有童真般的坦率，也具备成型音阶缺失带来的质朴专业感。开篇以繁忙城市街道的环境声构建基底，随后合唱元素与具体音乐式的声碎片彼此交融，形成层叠的织体。声音在即时的欢愉与缓慢弥漫的忧郁之间不断切换，色彩时而慵懒、时而触动人心、时而萦绕不去。推荐网址指向krysalisound.com，属于独立小众厂牌发行。整体来看，这是一张融合田野录音、无人机氛围与具体音乐手法的实验作品，对实验音乐和氛围音乐爱好者具有吸引力。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Merryn Jeann Fear Of The Beauty Parlour Australian singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist finds tenderness in fragments on her second album At what point does a song stop being a song? Strip away the beat, harmony and narrative; leave behind a voice, a melody, a few repeated words, the hiss of a phone recording. Merryn Jeann’s Fear Of The Beauty Parlour seems fascinated by precisely that threshold. Jeann has never been particularly interested in conventional singer-songwriting. In the Australian artist’s music, the voice can transform into an instrument, a simple melody can suddenly break off, and an intimate story can give way to a field recording, a strange synth sound or a seemingly random noise. On Dog Beach, producer Rob Ellis helped her organise these eccentric... The post Merryn Jeann – Fear Of The Beauty Parlour appeared first on The Quietus.

items._cn_summary: Merryn Jeann 的第二张专辑《Fear Of The Beauty Parlour》聚焦于歌曲解构的临界点——剥离节拍、和声与叙事后，留下嗓音、旋律、重复歌词以及电话录音的嘶嘶声。她将人声视作乐器，让简单旋律突然断裂，使私密叙事让位于田野录音、怪异的合成器声响与看似随机的噪音。制作人 Rob Ellis 协助她组织这些不拘常规的元素，使作品介于歌曲与声音艺术之间。这张专辑不追求传统的民谣叙事流畅度，而是用碎片化的声响结构营造亲密感，探索了流行与实验之间的灰色地带。
